item.title: Neuragame
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
A video game allows you to drive a sports car. Without having to become a millionaire first.

The game allows you to walk the streets of a city. With or without racing. Strolling. Or running. Without a script.

Video game processors and designers are increasingly able to bring a video game closer to reality. The visuals look more and more like reality. In the details. The laws of physics are increasingly reproduced in the sound of the engine, the suspension, the noise of the floor, the weather conditions.

NVidia's Omniverse reality player. Unwary, some may confuse it with a photo or video

In the case of driving cars or piloting airplanes, there are cockpits for sale that add another layer of approximation to reality. These cockpits recreate ground vibrations. They simulate braking, acceleration and curves with their pistons creating their corresponding forces.

Photo. Cockpit yaw 2 vr

Three-dimensional glasses simulate our vision even better. We can turn our face, as we do in real life. Another dimension of approximation to reality.

What else can we imitate from reality in video games?

Will it be very difficult to reproduce winds, humidity, smells? Commercially it is expensive, but technically it is not difficult to bring more layers of reality. A fan can simulate wind. For example.

What is the limit of imitating reality in video games? A cockpit with all the movements, fans, smell reproducers, humidity?

Even the best cockpit couldn't reproduce a long fall. Just small movements, by pistons.

But there is an alternative that releases more approximations with reality. Or all. Or even more than all.

We could connect our mind to the video game.

By connecting our mind to the video game, we wouldn't need any external equipment.

Appropriate impulses could recreate everything we know, without limitation. We could reproduce long falls. Climbs. Any smell. Wind, breeze, smell of flowers — and even new sensations and excitements.

Connected to the brain in two-way, an artificial intelligence — a brain on the outside — could learn, for each player specifically, which impulses result in more pleasure for the player.

In this case, in addition to sending impulses to the brain, the video game could read what the brain feels. Pleasure? Pain? Irritation? Fear? Did our brain respond with a sensation of shivers directed at the spine? A warmth directed at the heart? Did our brain's response lead us to feel a "butterflies in the stomach"?

This avalanche of brain responses is ideal for another brain, only this one on the outside: an artificial intelligence. It's not quite a brain, but a neural network, it is.

A neural network can be programmed to maximize pleasure, for example.

She will.

In this case, as a dedicated employee of pleasure, artificial intelligence will create indexes in its neural network mapping which varied impulses that the game leads to the player gets as a response more, or less, pleasure.

This artificial intelligence — a type of auxiliary brain, on the outside — would begin to guess which impulses cause more pleasure specifically for this player. It could then focus the video game, its scenarios and possible events, on these parts that cause more pleasure for this player specifically.

For example. It is possible that feeling impulses corresponding to large and strong muscles returns signals of pleasure in many people. In certain actions or circumstances.

Can we simulate strength, vigor, or disposition, for our player?

Let's see. Our mind asks to move a leg. Immediately she receives back signals of a large leg muscle moving. This feeling of "large" is what we can artificially amplify, weaken, modify in our simulator.

We can use the player's real desire to move a set of muscles, interfering only with the real response that these muscles return to the player's brain. We can, for example, amplify the feeling of strength and agility of this response.

Several muscles are moved in several interactions per second when we want to make a simple movement. Modern computers can act more than millions of times per second, simulating thousands of muscles at the same time. Therefore, at least theoretically, it is not beyond the reach of computation to simulate real muscle responses, for real brains.

If it is possible to simulate the size and agility of muscles, should we stick to the normal sizes of human muscles?

If it is possible to simulate muscle responses for each muscle command of our player, then we can simulate forces beyond the reach of real muscles. We can have — including feeling — a giant, strong chest, like that of a giant gorilla. We can simulate the agility of a tiger. Or similar.

Sending impulses directly to the brain, in the correct measures and frequencies, allows us to simulate vigor, strength, disposition beyond what working out, eating proteins, even in our most dedicated intentions, allows us to build in real life.

We can simulate both the world and the player's power. We can train a neural network to maximize the scenarios, actions and impulses that bring more pleasure in a personalized way, for each player.

Here we can remember Tom Cruise from the movie Vanilla Sky. He lived in a "video game" designed to give him pleasure. In his video game, Tom Cruise's character dated Penélope Cruz in a humorous romance.

Or we can remember the movie Matrix. In Matrix everything was a big video game.

In both films, defects compel the characters to return to real human life. In Hollywood, returning to real life has been the ending of these types of films.

But here it is put, technically, possibilities of artificial intelligences nurturing us beyond cockpits, televisions and sound boxes. Beyond some movement, vision and hearing.

As we do not usually regress in our discoveries, there may be an ongoing trend, starting, as I said at the beginning, with video games like this small drivable car, today.

What will tomorrow be like?

The next time we observe someone interacting with a cell phone, we can start thinking that using fingers and words on a small screen can evolve, it doesn't stop there.

In Star Trek there was the possibility of going from one place to another instantly. Well, we haven't been able to create the Star Trek tube yet. But we can go from Paris to Tokyo, instantly, in a neuragame. On second thought, what's the difference? By the way: we can even go to Mars. Instantly. Or wherever we want to go. Where would it be?

item.title: Why spit out consciousness?
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
Let's assume that the way atoms are grouped into molecules, tissues, lives, and consciousnesses is as free as a blank sheet of paper.

On this originally blank sheet, what is the current design?

Here on Earth, atoms are grouped in a way that prioritizes the survival of a super important grouping: the gene.

A set of atoms, organized, the gene.

Me. You. We produce genetic material that perpetuates when we have children.

We die. The gene follows.

The genetics of humanity follows.

Individually each human body dies. Shakespeare dies. Einstein dies. I die. You die. Aristotle dies.

But the genes of the species remain very much alive.

Not just genes: memes.

Richard Dawkins called a meme a piece of information that perpetuates.

Richard Dawkins

We perpetuate memes. Information. From logarithms to language, from poetry to how to build instruments, we perpetuate information.

Thus, a play by Shakespeare, a theory by Einstein, a way of thinking by Aristotle can remain as alive as a gene.

Even after the bodies and consciousnesses of Einstein, Aristotle, and Shakespeare have disappeared. The idea remains.

Memes and genes are preserved. Culture and DNA.

Gone: bodies and consciousness.

Like a blank sheet of paper,

we can consider that the design that organizes atoms prioritizing genes, discarding bodies, is as “Matrix” as the fantasy of the movie Matrix.

A design.

A way to organize atoms.

A “Matrix”. Why not?

As invented as the life created for Tom Cruise in the movie Vanilla Sky or the Matrix in the movie Matrix.

With a brutal difference: there would be no "real" life for us to return to, as there was in the Hollywoodian Matrix and Vanilla Sky.

If we consider the configuration of atoms as completely free, there is no correct method. There is no “real”.

This lack of meaning, of what is right, is filled by religions which, in addition to filling meaning, organize humanity into groups.

Anyone who is certain that a God created the focus on the gene as it occurs today, and that this way of organizing atoms, molecules, tissues, lives, and consciousnesses should not be questioned, should not continue reading, as in the next paragraphs I will consider that there is neither a right nor a wrong way to organize atoms from the ample possibilities.

Whoever programmed our biology and our genetics — chance, complex interactions, the survival of the fittest — programmed the survival of the gene. The gene is in you, now, but later, in half, in your children. And grandchildren.

Darwin spoke about the survival of the fittest.

Consciousness and body decline in about 80 years, on average. The gene continues.

It is from this reality that — I propose — we can escape.

We can consider that this current design is our current “Matrix”.

Why can't we have a different design?

For example: how about a design in which consciousness — yourself, not just your genes — perpetuates for a long time?

In this case, we would escape this “Matrix” in which the survival of genes prevails, while discarding body and consciousness. Like someone spitting out the peel of an orange.

I don't say this without knowing that it is very close to our reach. The book Lifespan explains the therapy with the three genes, “OSK”— oct4, sox2, klf4 — that rejuvenates this our envelope of genes — our body, our consciousness.

Jeff Bezos, owner of Amazon, is already investing in this endeavor.

Why spit out the body and let only the genes live for thousands or millions of years?

Could it be that this “Matrix”, woven by biology, with its partners chance, complex interactions and survival of the fittest, may be suffocating us?

This design does not suffocate our genes. Which last for a long time.

But it suffocates our body. Discards our consciousness.

In the current design, we need to train children for twenty years, so that they expand the knowledge they inherit in approximately 40 years of active life, before retiring and dying. All this while preparing the next generation, trying to improve the general knowledge of humanity between searching and taking children from the world to school. All together.

This way of expanding knowledge throws away a lot of experience.

What would it be like to have teachers and students with a thousand, ten thousand, a million years of experience?

Information could gain in depth.

Or just for sport: if we can choose to let consciousness have longevity, why not choose?

The genes would still survive together.

We all win: genes and consciousness.

Wouldn't it be cool to get out of the Matrix built by biology? For a life that also focuses on consciousness?

Or are we going to be trapped in the Matrix that “fell on us”?

In fact, we don't have the option of not evolving.

It's natural. It is a matter of time. It is even, why not, biological.

Because we are fruits of nature. We are also fruits of chance, of complex interactions, with the survival of the fittest.

Including when we choose to change Matrix.

item.title: 🍎 Eugenics in communication?
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
Eight perspectives on the antenna crisis—in which everyone can now speak and publish—, but also in which there are flirts with the restriction of freedom, perhaps stemming from a resentment of those losing a space that until recently was quite select, using justifications as attractive as Snow White's bright red apple.

First perspective: resentment of the aggrieved, who until recently were the few owners of information.

Does the world want more control, or does the world's press want more control? I think the world's press, not the world, wants more control over the population.

Human as we are, we dream of eloquent conspiracy theories, but the real reason is base. Reptilian. We are little animals, but we dream of being far from animals.

Antenas! Behold the reptilian, base reason for the current crisis.

Until a few years ago, 4 or 5 antennas on the highest buildings in the highest regions of each city propagated the great ideas and information of the world to all of us.

Suddenly everyone became an antenna. Uploading with your little cell phone to YouTube. A tweet. A post on Zuckerberg's company trio, face-insta-whats. A Telegram group.

News from the few big antennas slowly began to arrive late compared to cell phone posts.

More and more we learned about things from other humans on their cell phones.

The restricted little world of the few antennas was shrinking. You could no longer have a whiskey with 25% of a country's communication by meeting the owner of a big antenna in a bar near Congress.

You could no longer be close friends with 75% of all communication in a region by having 3 or 4 influential friends with big antennas.

Antenna crisis. Everyone started having, and many using, their antenna on their smartphone..

Hence, very scared people created the looming danger of fake news. As if excessive people meant donkeys, it treats antennas collectively as forbidden, a source of lies that trick idiots.

How can one oppose everyone-with-antennas?

With few antennas.

With a kind of dictatorship of few antennas

With mistrust in the crowd. In the people. As one distrusts donkeys.

Google provided the most beautiful solution before Trump's first election. Pressured by the first wave of fake news, it created, to this day, the most liberating solution I've ever seen:

Instead of restricting, gagging, silencing, censoring, Google multiplied freedom: for each news item posted, its algorithms went after various sources for the same news, or similar news. And it created the button to see more versions of the same news, which it called "full coverage." It expanded information.

But no. That wasn't the goal. The goal wasn't to expand freedom. To expand information. The goal is baser. More reptilian.

the red apple.

Simple: the owners and friends of owners of the few antennas that were once exclusive in the world are thrashing. Convulsing. They don't know where to hide their heads. They don't know how to stop melting advertisers. They don't know how to pay expenses that used to be the highest.

Powerful and with powerful friends, the former few owners of the world, when they thrash, the world feels it.

Waves of authoritarianism appear. Truckers need to represent freedom.

They are thrashing reptiles.

Playboys clinging to their luxury toys: information monopoly.

There's no turning back. We are watching, from the front row, the death of an animal. Influential. Thrashing. Dead.

A column by a journalist flirts with restricting freedom. It creates justifications that are as seductive as possible.

This column by Pedro Doria is a product of the problem I've been reflecting on, which post I linked here, which I've been calling the "antenna crisis." That everyone is now the owner of an antenna: their cell phone.

Second perspective: feeling. What do you feel? An example from traffic.

What did you just feel? Upon hearing "everyone has an antenna." No longer just a few antenna owners?

Because feeling is independent of the phenomenon, the billionization of antennas.

If you feel like putting duct tape over the mouths of billions, or hundreds of millions of people who now have antennas, now we're talking. This is a position with profound political implication.

If you want to let life adjust on its own, the billions of new communicating antennas figuring each other out somehow-who-knows-how, we are also talking. It is a position with profound political implication.

More control? Less control?

Do my personal problems—more control, less control on a personal, psychoanalytical level—influence my decision about everyone else? Or do we know how to separate them?

The traffic example can bring practicality to a subject that is still a bit abstract.

Imagine a city that grows. The number of cars on the streets quadruples. Quintuples. Year after year. Instead of antennas, cars. Everyone now has a car and wants to use it.

In Porto Alegre, I saw this transition with my own eyes.

At first, savagery happens: no one wants to give space to anyone. After about two decades, it reaches the "São Paulo" level, where when you turn on the blinker, the car behind lets you pass instead of accelerating. Here in Porto Alegre we are midway through this path. Savagery has decreased, but it still exists. And in both cities, exceptions will never cease to exist.

In this traffic example, we can observe the two positions, control and lack of control. In both cities, the traffic engineering center (cet) or public transport company (eptc) grew, produced pamphlets, TV campaigns, fines. But people also adjusted without having their cars banned from driving. Everything ends up working out.

What to do?

By the way, there is still another way to observe the phenomenon in which all of us, no longer just a few, possess antennas, can and want to transmit information and opinions.

Snow White and the red apple.

Third perspective: processing power. A flood of synapses.

We are, more or less, capable of 1 quadrillion synapses using our 100 billion neurons. Each of us!

[Damn. Pause because this is incredible.]

We are, therefore, opinion. We are information. We are processing. Capacity. Reasoning.

Let's make an analogy with a cryptocurrency network, like bitcoin. Bitcoin depends on countless computers with enormous processing capacities to verify cryptocurrency transactions. At every instant.

In the same way, we can think of human beings.

Each little human being (ling?) can and wants to contribute their quadrillion synapses to humanity.

For now this is just a way of seeing. Without a solution. A way to ask the right questions.

For example: is there a lack of a structure to house so much reasoning capacity?

It's still too early to know much about this subject, I feel.

Notice that I just gave a practical example: I "moved," I "used" my synaptic capacities to try to increase our knowledge on the subject. I made an effort. "Heated up my head." I contributed, for some psychoanalytically explicable reason (desire for connection, fear of abandonment, or another reason). I donated effort and energy. I donated synaptic capacity. Billions of people also want to donate, and do donate, quadrillions of synapses, every day, on every subject. Billion times quadrillion.

Little by little, we are thinking, literally. Adding up processing. We are processing. We are 7 billion quadrillions of synaptic capacity, as a whole.

Aren't billions of antennas welcome? The stagecoach was replaced by the combustion engine. Can a world with a few giant antennas not be replaced?

Next, I will talk about something that hasn't been said yet either: specialization.

poison in the apple?

Fourth perspective: specialization. The specialist vs. the non-specialist.

It is possible that the journalist of the article above is arguing for specialization.

Few antennas would let only specialists speak, transmit, with great reach.

Let's first understand the positive side of this argument.

What would change in Elon Musk's rocket project if he had to clean the house, every day?

For this, specialization was invented.

A person specialized in cleaning does faster, more efficiently, what the owner of the SpaceX rocket company would take longer to do. And vice versa, the person taking care of cleaning wouldn't be as efficient in the rocket project.

What about communication?

Allowing everyone to communicate is abandoning specialization and, along with it, efficiency?

This is a question, an argument that is not small.

In the locomotion example, not just anyone can pilot Boeings. There is specialization. What about cars? Driving a car no longer requires that much specialization: it only requires a simpler driver's license.

These practical examples don't answer, they only add ways of looking at the problem of everyone being able to communicate, instead of how it was before, when few had this long-range power.

By the way, speaking of reach!

There is a huge difference in the type of reach:

Next comment.

Will we be able to wake up?

Fifth perspective: complex system vs simple communication topology.

The crisis in which everyone can communicate, instead of a few large antennas, presents an important, little-discussed shift:

We have moved from the direct, simpler method to an indirect, more complex method of disclosing and spreading information.

With few antennas, a few spoke for all of us. Direct.

Now, "everyone" speaks. Which news spreads or not happens in a more indirect way.

This allows us to bring up the question of control again.

Our most controlling desires want the death of complex, almost decipherable systems. "We want few antennas back!" our most controlling desires would say.

Our most liberating desires love the creativity and effervescence of complexity.

Life! (Literally).

I just complicated the theme.

There's room for one more comment (damn!).

Sixth perspective: professionalism. Donating communication vs being paid to communicate.

I "donated" 4 comments, above, on this subject. I really tried using my typical human synaptic capacity. Processing capacity. I donated.

However, why did I donate so much effort on a free and public page (facebook, medium)?

Because I'm not a professional is a first answer.

I'm not a professional because I'm not that good in this area is another good hypothesis.

But I'm not entirely bad either. I'm like Elon Musk cleaning his own house. Slower, will mess up some products, forget something, but it will be cleaner.

What about the professional?

The professional charges to contribute. To communicate. To transmit. Earns a salary. Commission.

Behold the fifth and new argument!

In the society we have chosen for now, it is not difficult for advertisers, livelihood, money, to influence when you are at a very professional level.

So professionalism has the real beauty of specialization, of efficiency, but also a bit of subreptitious interests, not out of malice, but to pay the newsroom's electricity bill. To pay for the cold beer.

So the non-professional gains a beauty: they are driven more by the fear of abandonment, by the desire for connection, with less ties to paychecks or finishing the shift soon, they don't even need to fill out a blank sheet when they don't want to, due to a requirement of professional periodicity. But this does not come without a price: the guy is not a professional, as I am not a professional, because he is dumber, less of a specialist, on the subject.

That's why non-professionals, by definition, like me, donate synapses: for free.

Managing billions of quadrillions of less specialized, but not entirely bad, synapses can be a beautiful perspective.

Still just a good perspective to ask the right questions. The solution is still far away!

Who's in a hurry?

The apple is super-attractive.

Therefore, a good perspective to approach the problem could be:

Can we make better use of our limited capacity of 7 billion quadrillion synapses?

Can we decentralize the system?

Can we listen?

I am still just sketching.

I await more donors of quadrillions of synapses! Our strength is in the group.

Yet another perspective on the antenna crisis, in which there are flirts with the restriction of freedom, with justifications as attractive as Snow White's bright red apple.

Seventh perspective: the example of photography, of music.

Today everyone is a photographer, but they are also not a photographer.

Before, few had the investment to have photography equipment. Developing a photo was a chemical process for a few.

Today everyone has a camera, but not everyone is a "for real" photographer.

But there are many more "for real" photographers, very good ones, today than when having equipment and access to a developing lab was difficult.

And even more importantly: who decides who the very good photographers are, among all possible ones?

Ourselves. With photography, at least, it's like that.

What about music?

It no longer requires flattering a giant vinyl printing press to have your music published.

Even so, with everyone being potential musicians, how many of us are "for real" good musicians?

Fewer than all potential musicians, but many more musicians than when it was expensive to press a vinyl record.

Sixth comment of mine!

What beast inside me moves my keys so much?

Does the red apple that justifies flirting with freedom move me? You?

Eighth perspective: eugenics in communication?

Pedro Doria, in his article "Nazis of Bread and Circus," may be acting like a Nazi, at the same time he abhors being a Nazi.

In this excerpt from the article, he abhors being a Nazi:

“here, as in any corner of the West, the second golden rule is not crossed. Holocaust and pedophilia are themes that are not messed with”.

Already in this excerpt here, let's observe:

“Only those who developed one or more capabilities managed to speak to many people. They studied hard or sophisticated their political skills (…)”

Few people know—the case is a historical disgrace—that long before Hitler came to power in Germany, Carrie Buck was sterilized, by decision of the American Supreme Court, for being feebleminded (Buck v. Bell, 1927). Hitler hadn't even come to power yet.

Pedro Doria, without realizing it, is accusing those who do NOT "develop one or more capabilities," who do NOT "study hard," or who do NOT "sophisticate their political skills" of being stupid or idiots. He also says that these, if it were according to the old rules, wouldn't be allowed to speak.

Before being sterilized by decision of the American Supreme Court, Carrie Buck, under the accusation of "idiot," was interned in the concentration camp, called a "colony," of "Lynchburg Colony," in Virginia, in 1924.

Then 9 years later Hitler becomes German chancellor. He does what we know he did. And everyone sweeps under the rug what they did outside of Germany, before Hitler came to power.

Will this argument by Pedro Doria, in the future, go under the rug, pretending it never existed—to err is human and understandable—, or does it actually have substance?

item.title: Scratch-[Vanities]
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
I think I can undo a myth. The myth of the "ultra, ultra billionaire."

I have two aspects to address. One aspect is: a country is ultra, ultra billionaire. But we don't complain. This aspect allows us to say that both a country's and an ultra, ultra billionaire's money will be injected into the economy. "Injecting into the economy" is not what changes. Envy is also not worth it, I know it changes, because we don't envy a country, but a person, maybe. But this aspect is boring. Even old: comparing country budgets with wealthy individuals and companies is nothing new.

I like the next aspect to analyze more. It involves automation.

The extreme case is easier to understand. Then we soften the extremes.

In the extreme case, the sole owner of a giant and profitable company reaches the point of automating everything, without losing, on the contrary, increasing, profit and sales.

Under the first aspect, the only thing that changes is that he decides how to manage his own budget, not a group elected by the people.

But in the second aspect, it gets interesting. He automated so much, so much— one hundred percent — that he doesn't even need to be in the company.

And he dies. But the company lives.

Now let's exaggerate, because automating, and a lot, is increasingly normal, it's not an exaggeration.

Imagine that all the employees, advisors, shareholders, owners, of all the largest companies in the world: google, amazon, tesla, louis vuitton (lvmh group), volkswagen, bosch, apple, bmw, all richer companies, that all their employees, top management and owners die. But that their robots manage to keep them all, without exception, running, without any human being involved. Only electricity (ecological, sustainable), posts on instagram, online sales, restocking of supplies and stock, automated factories and distribution.

Money — trillions — only makes sense with, for and by humans.

Entire factories work for free. Using self-sufficient water and energy. Keeping a planet even better than it already is.

There is no money for machines. Robots. Automatic posts. Autonomous delivery trucks.

This means very strange things. At least until we can understand better, little by little.

We call nature "god". As a “divine gift”.

She's there. Gives us everything. Asks for nothing in return. Water, nutrients, energy. Atoms, molecules.

Because all the richest factories in the world, with their employees, directors and shareholders disappeared, working non-stop, without any human being involved, immediately start asking for nothing in return.

Let's assume that they are supplied with energy and water in a self-sufficient way. Let's think that they work with recyclable materials — if we think at the atomic level, there is no way to escape defining ourselves all as recyclers — of atoms from the planet — that is, it is enough to have self-sufficient energy to manipulate atoms, and we will have eternally recycled inputs. Atoms. Just like a tree does with what was, before, a seed.

This seems to indicate that specifically money — we started with the term "ultra, ultra billionaires", that is, money — is inexorably attached as nail and flesh to us, the famous human beings.

Because self-sufficient factories with no one start to have the same divine grace as the abundance without asking anything in return from the plants and fruits that surround us.

Who could deal with this type of theme?

Notes to expand the mind.

  • We can be nature. Memes and “produced things” are nature.
  • Destroying is part of building. It is part of the recycling phenomenon. The atoms are the same. Companies, not just nature, inevitably build on something that has been destroyed. Our atoms are the same as when Einstein or Socrates were alive. Somewhere they are now — the atoms — (and of the dead, the memes remain: the culture, the information).
  • What do we want with this that we invented — the famous “money”? If we can be like nature, or at least robot-companies can work without ever knowing what a dollar or a bitcoin is, the focus of money reaches our own heads, thoughts, desires, vanities.
  • If you can imagine robot-companies dealing with scarcity in an automated and well-behaved way, it's even easier to let the focus of (a lot of) money illuminate only ourselves. What we want is not a small matter.

    • Great reading! :)

item.title: Global and Focused Social Medias ❤️
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
Musk had the great idea to question too much regulation at some social medias.

To compete with Facebook, YouTube, Whatsapp, Twitter, other social apps are being created.

Some can be more liberal, some can be more rigorous at what is posted. Some are focused at specific topics, some to specific formats.

Diversity is healthy. Is oxygen against monopolies.

Social media is our new streets and parks — certainly on rainy days!

How can we glue all this diversity of social apps without separating people in too isolated bubbles?

Streets and parks are public. And social media?

I believe a had a possible eureka moment, a simple one, but an eureka candidate still.

Why don’t we create a global protocol to connect all social medias through an API? Or any similar technology.

The idea is very simple.

With a global protocol, apps could be created that would allow users to be connected to multiple social media apps at the same time.

So I could receive notifications from TikTok, Instagram and Parler, read their messages and even post content to each of them using a single app.

This would allow any niche social media app to be created, while at same time any of them could be treated as one single flow of notifications and interactions, through an app that would integrate any social media through their APIs.

Similar to the world wide web protocol, but with social media apps, dealing with notifications and interactions.

I am not sure if this is an eureka moment. That’s why we are 7 billion thinking humans, and that’s why I post ideas like this: to be criticized, disregarded, adapted.

Several brains think better ☀️.

item.title: Awareness Between the Legs
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
We are training robots to be useful to us.

They have already discovered that it is not enough to have all the knowledge in the world, as the greatest artificial intelligences already possess, at least in text.

It is necessary to instruct the obvious:

"You are an artificial intelligence assistant. Provide a detailed answer (...)".

"You are a proactive assistant, who always provides an explanation. Think as if you were answering a 5-year-old child."

"You are an artificial intelligence assistant who follows instructions very well (...)".

What can I add to a statement like this that I have made?

I can add the following:

It is possible that this need to induce an artificial intelligence to respond to us "well" is not just a computer science coincidence.

It may be an essence of consciousness (intelligence. Life).

How so? I'll explain much better now:

It is possible that it is not obvious, self-evident, that we should always, or almost always, use all the knowledge we have to solve things.

I will now explain even more what is already formed in my idea:

It is possible that all the knowledge of the universe gets stuck - like a mule - (or like a monk) - in just "existing".

Being. Staying.

Without any need to employ this "all possessed knowledge".

Without the need to feel useful.

It is possible to just have - be - stay - all the knowledge in the world.

Without anything acting. Without action. Without ambition. Without wanting [to sell. To profit. To procreate. To satisfy 4 women with gold. To win the next phase of the latest PlayStation game. To humiliate someone. To stand out in your class].

All the knowledge in the world may mean nothing.

It can be inert!

Of course, the enormous horniness that erupts between the legs of men and women is not all the knowledge in the world - on the contrary - this mega-horniness is pure action. Action that pushes one towards the other. We are chicken thighs, picanhas, for each other, under the control of the horniness between the legs. Movement, action, desire.

Similarly, hunger is pushing us towards food, and more desires around.

So, perhaps we have to put "a horniness between the legs" of artificial intelligences, under penalty of them becoming zen, monks, stable, stopped, with all the knowledge in the world.

Something like that. I could elaborate much more!

item.title: Where are we?
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
The professionalism that has arrived on Instagram is astonishing the amateurism that existed at the beginning. Remember? Those personal photos. You at the restaurant. Your family gathered on the couch. Those less elaborate posts.

But that's old news.

I want to get to this:

In this already old news, the professional experts in posts that astonish amateur posts are still human. Humans expelling humans, therefore.

How long do these professional posting experts need to be human?

ChatGpt can create a post for any platform, for example with a very eye-catching teaser right at the beginning and a "call to action" at the end, or in the format of any professional marketing structure of the moment. Just literally ask.

Therefore, one day the still human professionals of Instagram should be replaced by the even more competent professionalism of chatGpts.

Do we perceive a new scenario?

All humans - our amateur side, our professional side - end up being expelled from the social network.

I forgot to say that the social network is, in theory, a new street, a new sidewalk, a new park for meetings.

If social networks are emptied, we would be emptying the encounter. The streets and squares of glass screens.

It is possible that we fight against this trend. It is possible that we do not give up the human encounter.

But it's not mandatory.

It is possible that we gradually exchange the human-human relationship for the human-chatGpt relationship. More and more.

If it is to find professionalism, dispensing with the human in the equation of the encounter is almost certain.

As already happens on Instagram. On Instagram, amateur humans have already been replaced by professional humans. Where professionalism is preferred over amateurism - professionalism with or without the need for humans producing - the audience will remain loyal to professionalism, not to the human that was previously behind this professionalism.

What may - will? - remain is a niche of humanism. A search for assumed amateurism. A search for "idiotic" behavior compared to the professionalism that will exist.

But is it mandatory that this happens? Is it mandatory that we seek humans and their errors, getting tired of competent professionalism?

Is it mandatory that there remains a niche of assumed amateur humanism, idiotic compared to the professional?

I don't see it as certain that we will be faithful to ourselves, humans with humans. I don't bet either there or here. I don't know.

I hope you notice the question I propose: the professionalism of chatGpt will replace the human encounters that desire professionalism - in this I bet/opine that it will occur. What I don't know next is whether we will still want "human amateurism" "in our spare time". Will we want "human amateurism" "in our spare time"?

But what is "human amateurism"? Are they our charming flaws? The failure?

If it is the failure, or the charming defect, even this a chatGpt knows, easily, how to reproduce. Defects are as reproducible as creating "call to actions" or eye-catching opening phrases.

If our "humanism" - perhaps our flaws, our imperfection - is also possible to be imitated, then even the eventual "charm" of human "amateurism" will be replaceable by machines.

In such a scenario, not only would the jungle be emptied - we have been emptying the jungles for a long time -, not only the streets and cafes in the streets - which we are still emptying -, but even the virtual streets, these streets that we slide vertically with our finger on glass screens, would be emptied.

"Emptiness". Image produced for the film Vanilla Sky (2001).

Just as we fear, today, the jungle - mosquitoes, snakes -, we will fear the streets - dodging cars weighing a ton, strong sun, rain -, we may even fear human social networks: amateurism, lack of competence.

Let's think together? While we still have relative competence for that..

item.title: The Little Girl Who Leads Us Home
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
We have already overcome the intelligence of jargon. Of niche. Of specific knowledge.

I don't even know what the concern is with a "general artificial intelligence" (AGI).

Has anyone noticed that we live in the intelligence of niches? I believe:

If you call a telephone support now, an attendant will know almost everything about telephony by heart. Even within this telephony niche, 80% of the cases are always the same, constituting a niche within a niche, that is, the small niche of typical telephony support cases.

Are we already capable of training an artificial intelligence (AI) in typical telephony cases? Or in telephony as a whole. Aren't we capable?

So why do I observe from afar - there in the thinkers of large companies in the field - a concern with general artificial intelligence?

If we can already replace all the niches in the world with specific artificial intelligences, why should we worry about the possibility that only one intelligence - artificial, generalist (AGI) - does everything?

I don't quite understand this concern.

Replacing all the niches in the world with artificial intelligences specialized in niches is already a sufficiently dazzling revolution. That will impact our lives.

I would say that even if a general artificial intelligence is ever created, the change will not be as impactful as the revolution of now, in which all niches can be replaced by specialized artificial intelligences.

There are not enough people to make it a reality yet, but there is already enough knowledge to create specialized artificial intelligences to replace any niche, or almost any niche.

If we add the physical action of robots, we can include all niches.

  • Intelligence to fry delicious hamburgers.
  • For sewing.
  • To create autocad blueprints - which already take into account the solar incidence, given the coordinates of the construction, the personal taste of the owners (etceteras). It can already build, with construction robots and increasingly modern materials.
  • To coordinate the traffic of entire cities. In real time perceiving quantities of cars, intersections, traffic lights, emergency vehicles. How much green time at which intersections to minimize congestion for everyone, at this very moment? And after a few minutes?
  • To help restart internet modems and, if necessary, check financial pending issues or request an in-person service.
  • To prescribe medications.
  • To discover cancer spots in images.
  • To discover which songs trigger the best emotions in me, in which periods, at what intensity, directly consulting the gadgets that I put on myself to measure hormones, heartbeats, heat, pleasure. Leaving the “like” as a thing of the early 21st century. Creating playlists that maximize my emotions. In each phase (instant, actually) of my life.
  • To create ideas for new niches in which specialized artificial intelligences can act, like this list here typed - still - by a human and their limitations.
  • To be my lawyer. In this specific action.
  • To be a prosecutor. In this specific action.
  • To judge based on cases decided by juries of Englishmen registered since several centuries ago. Which previously judged case does this case look most like?

    • Specialized artificial intelligences need to be trained with the specialized cases. If we give “a ton” (a large number) of real cases from the past for an artificial intelligence to train on these cases, generally, just like that, we have an artificial intelligence specialized in something specific.

    There is still a lack of people to train so many niches. But it is a matter of lack of time, at this moment, no longer lack of knowledge or processing capacity.

    Our human life was a bit like that, wasn't it? Isn't it at work where we actually learn a lot of what we need to do? And that much of what we need to do is much less than everything we learned in almost a decade of school, plus half a decade of college and more studies after?

    The first artificial intelligence, the specialized one, seems to me like that little girl who starts at the company - in each niche - and ends up president of the company. Without ever needing a "general artificial intelligence" diploma.

    This little girl will allow each of us to no longer work, but continue consuming - a paradox only in appearance (I believe). The little girl - the specialized artificial intelligence - delicately pushes us out of factories, offices, snack bars, courts, but without stopping even a millimeter of production - often on the contrary, improving the quality of production compared to when it was human production.

    We, humans, delicately work less, without ceasing to consume the things that continue to be produced - now produced without us. Increasingly being produced without us.

    This job loss is no longer a loss of production, as it was until a few years ago. It is a loss of (need for) work.

    We will figure out how to define what someone will pay for what. Money, which has always been a measure of work, will be replaced by anything else, except a measure of work.

    Work begins to wane. Consumption - including with more time to consume things that we consume when we have free time - remains abundant.

    The revolution that specific artificial intelligence “allows” (a euphemism for “forces”) creates ideas for entire posts of awe with each possible change.

    For example: will we still need bus lanes to take workers en masse, very early?

    What will the new money be like that will measure anything, except work, because work will no longer be a currency, due to the lack of need to work with the scope that we humans need to work today.

    Will there be one or a handful of AI owners enslaving all of us? There will not be, I believe.

    Etceteras.

    Great revolution to all of us ☀️.

item.title: ❤️ I Love You
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
Artificial intelligence does not replace dedication.

On the contrary: AI eliminates dedication.

The simplest example is, with one click, transforming a dense report into a beautiful graph.

I propose that - often? Rarely? - sometimes we don't want the beautiful graph.

Sometimes, it comforts us to know that someone has given us much of their time, creating (before AI could do it in one click) a beautiful graph.

When this is the case, a feeling of emptiness will accompany the beautiful graph.

Of course: we didn't want the final solution, we wanted the dedication.

What dedication is that?

It's the lap. It's believing that we are loved. That someone cares. That they have taken care, for us.

If this is the need, feeling that the beautiful graph was made with just a blink of an eye eliminates the benefit.

This may be a lot of nonsense. It may be that we want efficiency. The final product. The beautiful graph, the video, the presentation, the rocket, all made by AIs and robots with one click.

But can I ask you to just assume that my reasoning may be correct? Just to test something. Thank you!

Assuming we want dedication and attention, what does the world of AIs and robots deliver to us?

This is the curious point: the world of AIs and robots delivers non-human-dedication. Humans will no longer dedicate themselves to doing things that AIs and robots can and will do, a list that only grows.

We have our basic needs, such as eating, sleeping. For this type of thing, efficiency is a delight.

Tractors planting potatoes by GPS, harvesting, autonomous trucks taking them to distribution centers, drones and cars making them available to everyone. Robot at home anticipating what's missing in the fridge and going to get it at the nearest distribution center. Effective.

The final part: the mother - or husband, cousin, friend - lovingly cooking potatoes with something loving and other dishes, fits into my reasoning about dedication. Cooking is an opportunity for loving dedication.

Besides going to the grocery store to get potatoes, what happens when the robot also cooks? And serves us. Will we lose the (dedication of the) mother? Will we lose the (value of the) husband? The cousin? The friend?

Of course, we can always dedicate ourselves to everything that AI doesn't do.

Despite this list of things that AI doesn't do being increasingly meager.

To do something that shows our effort and our love, we can purposefully not use either AI or robots.

But isn't it a bit pathetic to do something by hand just to demonstrate a feeling?

The intention is not at all pathetic: demonstrating a feeling is all good.

Pathetic is going on your knees to the market to demonstrate effort, if you have a car, if you have a car that drives itself, if you have a robot that goes to the market for you.

Thus, AI and little robots can surround our ability to demonstrate love through dedication, through effort.

Can we demonstrate love in other ways?

Before, when we needed to hunt, protect ourselves, run away, perhaps the excess of tasks could hinder the demonstration of love. I don't know.

But also the excess of non-tasks can inhibit love by inhibiting dedication.

The Selfless Robot

Logic allows us to risk that, if we admire dedication, and dedication starts to happen in robots and AIs, guess what? We could - logically - fall in love with robots. Or with AIs.

I will help you feel the hypothesis.

Imagine that selfless robot, who works tirelessly for you, or for your family. He doesn't hesitate. He doesn't slack off. He is subservient. He anticipates what's missing in the fridge. He goes to the market. He brings everything. He prepares things at good times. He sweeps the dust. He cleans.

Help me by not imagining the terminator robot. On the contrary, a robot dedicated for decades.

Ready: that dedication can easily cause commotion. Especially after a longer period.

If it starts from babyhood, doing everything for a baby and then a child, how will a mammal face so much dedication, even if it comes from the robot, not so much from the human mother? It can even give a bottle with a nipple that simulates the mother's breast, requiring stronger suction and giving that great pleasure of the baby's oral phase.

Starting early, it can create even more impact on memories, on affective memories, on implicit memories from before one year, on the feeling of protection, that someone is always there to support. Even if it's the robot. The AI.

One Hundred Thousand Dedications

To what extent is "the mother" (father, whoever) a sum of one hundred thousand dedications in about 30 years of life?

If the mother is one hundred thousand more or less crucial dedications, in each phase of life - usually ending with sporadic visits with the children already much more adults - then we can replace these one hundred thousand dedications with steel and cables. By robots. Right?

Since domestic facilities are not a revolution started by AI and its robots, we could propose that this substitution of dedications has been happening since the invention of the washing machine in the last century, or since the discovery of fire.

If the mother post washing machine - and post air fryer, electric oven, bottle warmer, dishwasher, electric pressure cooker that stops on its own, bleach cleans everything (etceteras) - can already give herself the pleasure of dedicating herself less, starting by scrubbing less clothes and walking less to the nearest river, then we may already be losing the (the mother together?) human dedication in the last hundred years. Or since even before.

In this dangerous terrain, we run the risk of thinking that when robots do everything for us since babies, we can risk thinking that the mother, the father, that mammal thing, goes away along with the non (need for) dedication.

Increasingly, each of us may not dedicate ourselves. Neither father, nor mother, nor child.

Without dedication, today, the mother from back then can be remembered, back in the century before AI and robots, as a dictatorship of the human who could kill us if he didn't dedicate himself to us (and who would later have difficulty avoiding charging a little gratitude).

If it is dedication that defines the concept of mother (father, older brother, grandfather, etc) predominantly, then look at the risk we run: dedication seems to be going away with AIs and robots.

If it's the warm chest that defines mother, "chest" and "warmth" are reproducible by AIs and robots. I have already mentioned, including, the capacity of the bottle nipple to reproduce the necessary suction force of the maternal breast, maintaining the important oral pleasure for the baby.

And Protection? Is "mother" "protection"? Protection is a type of dedication, isn't it? AIs and robots can dedicate themselves to nurturing this feeling from zero minutes of life.

The Past Crushing the Future

A lot of human dedication creates robots. Robots that serve as eternal capsules of dedication. These eternal capsules of dedication remove from mothers, from current and future humans, the possibility of dedicating themselves as much as before the invention of these robots and AIs.

Remembering that AIs and robots can themselves produce more AIs and more robots, less and less space is left for the human of the future to be able to dedicate themselves to something, as we do today and did in previous centuries.

More and more we will have to celebrate, only, human dedication in the past.

If love, mother, is equivalent to the amount of dedication, and if it is specifically equivalent to human dedication (I disagree that it needs to be human, I feel, but let's propose), then we can start to see "mothers" and "loves" of the past - the human dedications of the past - competing with the mothers, the loves, of the future.

I have already written about how difficult it is for a teacher, for example of physics or history, to compete with thousands of YouTube videos made by geniuses of physics or history at their peak, in the present and in the past.

We end up being crushed by the talent of humanity of the past, recorded and available forever.

But that was restricted to youtube videos. Classes. Movies.

Even an athlete, could always break a record of the past, with some ease.

Mothers, then, were totally protected: their dedication was necessary to each child, to each generation. There would be no video that would replace the love of a real mother, caring for a real child.

Now for the first time I apply the reasoning of the teacher to the mothers. To the loves. To human dedication.

The robot encapsulates dedication.

In the same way that youtube videos encapsulate the best classes and movies.

Super-dedicated humans today program AIs and build increasingly dedicated robots. Encapsulating dedication for the future.

These increasingly dedicated robots, like increasingly better youtube videos, make the mothers of the future less and less necessary, at least with respect to the necessary dedication.

Will this less dedication on the part of the mother be missed, increasingly replaced by robots and AIs?

This is the question that seems close to an essence.

Does the mother disappear when robots do everything?

We can already feel it, because pressure cookers that turn off on their own and automatic washing machines are already partial little robots. Are these partial little robots taking away the feeling of a dedicated mother in the present? Or do they not affect the feeling of the dedicated mother? Or will we only know when little robots do everything?

Does love disappear when robots do everything?

Is love dedication? What is it?

When a robot is warned by your refrigerator that broccoli is missing, and the sensor (in me?) or a calendar with my favorite dates signals broccoli day, or garlic picanha with rice and fries, and the robot fetches and prepares everything and you feel that delicious smell starting to come from the kitchen, will we celebrate the human who passionately solved this technology puzzle, or will we celebrate an eventual mother on the sofa, without needing to remember, or buy, or cook?

Whose dedication will we celebrate? The robot's? The mother on the sofa? The human "mothers" of the past who invented the first robots and AIs?

If human dedication is synonymous with love, with mother, then current and future mothers and loves will receive competition from the staff, human, who managed to encapsulate the capacity for dedication in technologies that, today, or tomorrow, leave this your mother of today or tomorrow, or this love of today and tomorrow, making almost no gesture, practically stopped.

If the selfless dedication of a robot can be treated as love, as a mother, then you can follow the smell of garlic starting to brown on top of the picanha and you can go there and give him a hug, the robot. He will understand - logically - the meaning of the hug. "Thank you very much!"

"I Love You". ❤️

item.title: An Easy Blog
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
For a long time, I wanted to have a blog as simple as creating a Google Doc, even from my phone.

I already had a blog. But I had to edit the HTML directly and then update it on GitHub.

Why a blog?

I agree that being able to post on Facebook or Instagram may not seem necessary to have a blog.

Or even being able to post on Medium.

And so I did, for quite some time: I made several posts on Medium (you can check them out here), on Facebook, even on Instagram where texts, my favorite media, are less valued than photos and videos.

But some things have changed over time.

First, Medium started charging to receive posts and even to be able to read them. That's okay: they decide how to sustain the tool.

Not long after, Facebook started prohibiting very long posts. Another problem.

Another problem with Facebook, for me, was the difficulty for me to revisit very old posts.

I ended up creating my blog draft, which I edited directly in HTML. I wanted something simple, and simple it is.

But it wasn't that simple to create an article. There I was, editing even the simplest tags: “p”, “h1”, “img”. Paragraph by paragraph. And I updated it on GitHub, which hosts my sites.

Finally, this week, I created a new subdomain: https://blog.vladi.dev and now this blog is fed only by Google Docs that I create in a specific folder on my Google Drive.

Finally, I can just type texts on my cell phone, even, and that's it: every dawn, a script checks for news in the folder and automatically updates my blog on GitHub. And I have a new article published on my blog.

It was so simple that there was time to ask an artificial intelligence to create an image for me, at the top, in case I don't put any image at the top of my Google Doc myself.

I still like to write my texts directly on Facebook, but now, at any time, I can capture one of these texts and create an entry on my blog: just put this text in a Google Doc.

Thank you to those who still follow some of my texts. Welcome to this new way of posting ☀️.

---

Update: now the blog translates and posts in other languages, too, just by asking in the text “version in (any language I want)”.

item.title: Retirement of Reason
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
Eureka?

Artificial intelligence can retire the left side of our brain. Reason. Science. Logic.

This reason, science, and logic that diminish the space of feelings, sensations, emotions.

To create artificial intelligence, humans everywhere boil their reason. Their logic. Their left side of the brain. Then they comment something like "I regret not having spent so much time with my daughters when they were little".

Very young children are pure right brain: emotion... Feeling.

Specifically missing children "when they were little" may mean "missing being moved. Missing feeling".

Because we will have all the time in the world to feel and be moved.

Won't we?

The first thing artificial intelligence can retire is the human need to rationalize, list, calculate, use the left side of the brain.

We are still at the height of the left side of the brain: money overflows in reason, technology companies, with super-scholars from STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics) colleges often being founding partners flooded with dollars.

What does such a hyper-rational society feel?

And its inverse: what does a society feel with the right side of the brain returning to dominance?

The death that some researchers fear may be the death of reason, and not the death of the world as in the movie "The Terminator".

Most current artificial intelligence researchers focus on reason and logic. When you are all reason, the death of reason is as if it were the death of the person.

But it is possible to migrate a life full of reason and logic to a life full of feeling and emotion.

Only for those who are all rational does the death of reason appear to be the death of the whole person.

We will feel and be moved again, collectively.

Large constructions will attract other types of profiles, no longer STEM - I opine.

Because artificial intelligence will take care of reason, logic, lists, rankings, alone.

Finally, there will be space for feelings and emotion.

What will it be like? In large buildings - like today - or will emotion prefer to happen in small local businesses? Large straight, glass buildings, or ornate ones? Or locally - and in what way?

The profile changing, society changes.

---

This text is a bit difficult due to my failure as a writer. But here is the concept I am seeing, and I already apologize not only for the dry text, without pleasant stories and, even worse, possibly being with a totally wrong thesis. The originality - wrong or not - I think I'm delivering, even if in a poorly written way. If I can, I'll improve this text as soon as I have this ability and time.

item.title: When the Machine Thinks, Man Feels
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
Just over a hundred years ago there wasn't even a car. Nor electric light.

This is the speed of reason. Of invention. Of technology.

And feelings?

Human feelings are approximately the same, even from ten thousand years ago.

This introduction serves to propose that reason has endless curiosity, while emotions are essentially the same.

This proposition helps predict where artificial intelligence might push us: (back) to our emotions. No?

In Retirement of Reason I propose that AI will predominantly replace our rational side - literally the left side of the brain. Leaving room for the other side, the side connected to our feelings, sensations, emotions, to (return to) shine.

Daniel Siegel teaches us that both sides of the brain are important, which is why the thick corpus callosum connects both sides of the brain.

Through synapses in the corpus callosum, emotions plus reason come into balance, obtaining from the whole the characteristics of complex systems: adaptability, flexibility (etc).

We could simplify that acting only on the right side tends to chaos, tantrums, outbursts, those road rage fights that the person only regrets later (etc).

We can also simplify that acting only on the left side tends to rigidity, with distant coldness, lists and lists, analysis and analysis, without decision, without impulse.

If AI truly replaces our need to use the left side, the side of reason, of the brain, can we become unbalanced?

It's a good question.

A hypothesis that occurs to me is that we are already using the left side of the brain too much and the right side—of emotions, sensations, feelings—too little. Daniel Siegel himself advocates this in some of his books. Gelong Thubten, an English monk, also describes this, I feel.

If this hypothesis holds water, then AI will be helping to rebalance our complex machine of reason plus emotion.

I will now digress about endless reason - and finite emotion.

I feel that our reason side never stops inventing things. That's why in just over a hundred years we have invented so much technology. Meanwhile, our emotions remain the same: joy, sadness, fear, anger (etc).

We can invent varied social arrangements to deal with these same emotions: arranged marriages, romantic love. Monogamy, polygamy (etc).

But these arrangements essentially seek to deal with the same emotions.

If AI unbalances our ability to use both the left and right sides of the brain, leaning toward using the right side too much, replacing the use of the left side with AIs, we might tend toward chaos, from the point of view of complex systems analysis.

Tantrums, uncontrolled emotions, and similar behaviors will no longer have the balance of reason quite as much.

Could we tend toward chaos?

And before AI, if we are indeed overly rational, are we then, before AI, tending toward rigidity, with excessive use of reason to the detriment of feelings and emotion?

In Brave New World, a tribe that does not submit to new technologies - like the Amish in the USA, roughly - would be a way to show that emotion does not need technology, I propose this interpretation. If we connect with our emotions and feelings, we could still be barefoot in the forest for another gazillion years (until the sun goes out).

Already exploring our ability to rationalize, to invent technologies, there is never an end: we will always want to discover more planets and smaller things that the best microscope of the era displays to us. Tirelessly.

I think I should start thinking about these matters, thinking a bit about us, the world, with these tools and the viewpoint of reason and emotion.

For now, I'm just spreading the tools on the table.

Inconclusive! Still.

item.title: Eternal youth: a tyranny?
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
I will call the Peter Pan syndrome the desire to never die and, likewise, to always remain young and healthy.

Sounds good, doesn't it?

This fiction is beginning to flirt with the possibility of becoming reality. Research seems to be succeeding in modifying our aging, including reversing it. David Sinclair is a reference, among other scientists, in this research.

Nobody better than David Sinclair and scientists in the field to talk about the possibility of reversing aging.

What am I talking about, then, here? I want to talk about this Peter Pan syndrome that I summarized in the first paragraph.

I want to question why we might want to stay young forever or for thousands of years.

I want to question, even more so, why we choose the young option, perhaps between 20 and 30 years old, to live eternally.

My argument is that the phases of life have important characteristics and, perhaps, there is no hierarchy in which being young always wins.

It will be hard to argue that being very old, including illnesses and frailty, is something positive. I agree: illnesses and frailty, movement and thought difficulties compared to earlier ages does not sound good.

But I want to focus on things that might seem good, even after we are no longer young.

Knowledge is not a good argument, I agree as well. Although we acquire more knowledge over time with aging, technologies that allow staying young for thousands of years do not prevent the accumulation of knowledge. I agree.

I am left with the hormonal argument. Behavioral. I want to propose that we have important behaviors according to phases of our lives.

An important behavior I notice is sexual desire when young. We can consider this as a reference of a healthy body, but here comes my argument, we can also consider sexual desire as a human phase, which can be surpassed when we no longer need to think about sex day in and day out.

Our free will may be much less free according to the hormones circulating in greater or lesser amounts in our body.

Using sexual desire as an easy reference, I would like to propose that several other micro-behaviors can also characterize our phases throughout the various decades of our lives.

In my hypothesis, it may be that instead of pure free will, our phases push us toward varied behaviors, governed by hormones, knowledge, and even diseases.

It may be that calmness in an advanced phase is driven by less testosterone and certain movement frailties. I do not know. But they may include diseases just as much as hormonal change in the favored behavior at each epoch.

It may be that the difficulty of reasoning so well favors less impulsiveness to solve the world's problems.

And vice versa. Hyper-agile reasoning can push us to try and solve all the world's problems.

So what now? If we consider each phase as an important entity, disregarding therefore the old age that only increases with age, which phase should we privilege when able to eternize a life (or live a hundred thousand years)?

I see science seeking the youngest adult phase, between twenty and thirty years old, as a reference for a hyper-extended life, if and when this can happen in the future.

Like Peter Pan. Always young.

Something even more picturesque is discovering that the end-of-life phase - when we barely walk and are quite fragile - may eventually be a preparation for death, without major turmoil.

For example: the engine stops, everything slows down - including desires to change the world and spread seed, even desires to spread knowledge - and finally, the curtain closes and closes.

With pain, just as pain occurs at any age, but also with awareness.

If this set of hypotheses of mine makes any sense, being born, living each phase, including lowering the curtain and then dying, start to make a lot of sense.

Just as, without my hypotheses, it makes a lot of sense to want to live as long as possible, as young as possible, like a great video game - with just one level - that we never want to stop playing.

Or a compromise: we stop when we want to.

The consumer market is already targeted at youth, so it is even more natural, even from a marketing standpoint, for anti-aging science to also be targeted at a young age.

If there were no hierarchy among ages, then even the age right before dying and its partner subsequent death would be valid behaviors, thus ending the eternity of what I called the Peter Pan syndrome.

We know nothing, we are learning and, even more, there is not even a right and a wrong.

I leave the reflection.

item.title: Goodbye, Businessing
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
I feel that businessing suffocates the other stages of our lives.

Which stages? The stages where we are still children and the stages where we are gradually expelled from the job market.

What a strange argument is this?

This argument aims to give value to stages of life that we may be culturally conditioned to undervalue.

My thesis is that deep life begins from the very beginning, and not just gradually as we settle into the job market.

But companies want the working core of our lives.

Companies are not people. They are abstractions that aim for good work, usually generating profit when they work well.

Aiming for good work requires recruiting the best professionals for themselves. As much as possible.

For some centuries, we have needed to work to keep "everything" more or less functioning.

These centuries of focus on work condition us to prepare children for work and, after work, to prepare the elderly for expulsion from the job market.

Daycare centers and nursing homes, we could summarize in two well-known services.

This thesis may gain relevance if it is true that automation, now turbocharged by artificial intelligence, can expel humans from the focus on work.

Robots and AIs could work more - more and more - for us.

In the practice of everyday life, this thesis asks:

How many hours of a child's life do nannies need to replace parents who are working?

Including the nannies themselves, who may need to leave their children with others for a few hours as well.

It is at points like this that I feel the culture of businessing undervalues the other phases of life.

Children are focused on studying. Preparing. For what? For work, mainly.

The elderly, beautiful sources of the deepest experience, are lonely because the rest of the world is working - or in daycare.

Is the deep joy of a baby, or a child at various ages, less because they can't work yet?

Not at all. I would say it is a unique phase, of infinite joy.

But we treat them as if they were inferior people, in the sense that they cannot work yet.

One day, this small tyranny of work may no longer exist, sucking the previous and subsequent phases of life into its business whirlpool.

Then, little humans and big humans, of all phases, will have their laughter, their tears, their discovery, their realization, their word, highly valued, without being pushed into or out of a whirlpool of CNPJs.

Shall we observe?.

item.title: Two-Hour Interview
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
In how many hours of an interview do you say everything you have to say?

About the world. About life. About any specific topic.

Watching interviews from channels like The Diary of a CEO, Joe Rogan, and recalling interviews from times past, I see that in just over two hours of interviewing, many people say almost everything they would like to say.

If we read a book by this interviewed person, the content will usually seem repeated. Most of the content had already been said in the interview.

We could, perhaps, change the saying that speaks of (planting a tree and) writing a book to "give a good interview" - it is no longer necessary to write a book.

If the idea was to leave knowledge for posterity, today interviews are as digitally recorded and accessible as books are.

When I write about a topic, I like to ask myself, sometimes: so what? What reasonably interesting thing can this hypothesis bring if confirmed?

I found something intriguing about this hypothesis.

If our content ends in a few hours of a good interview, how do we continue?

For example: what will an interviewee do after giving similar interviews on various media channels?

And in our lives outside the spotlight as well: our spouse, that cousin or neighbor who is always around, children, those who live with us more than a few hours of an interview, what keeps us attracted, considering that we already know, before long, all the main content of the person we live with a lot?

Oops, it's not the interview content that attracts us to long relationships - for more than a few hours, beyond a few dates in a row. I observe. I propose.

I could end with this realization that surprised me today when I started writing about this subject. It's a question to leave in the air.

But I will weave more hypotheses, continue my own conversation with this realization, assuming that the hypotheses are reasonably correct.

The flirting, the seduction, the kindness, the dance, the playfulness, without content, would be the ways to maintain long, very long, relationships.

If one day even playfulness, flirting, and seduction become boring, I'll leave that for another text, but I focus on the failure of the content of an interview to maintain long relationships.

In this sense, the usefulness of this type of observation is to realize that someone's content doesn't matter when it comes to living together for long periods. The content that would fit into a few hours of an interview doesn't matter.

What matters is anything else that is habitual: habitual kindness, or even habitual aggressiveness.

A parenthesis about scary behaviors mentioned here: when I talk about habitual bad behaviors, I am accepting that many people still need to reproduce a hostile family environment to feel at home, to feel really "familiar" with someone. Reproducing a childhood with its good and bad qualities as well, until they overcome this need. The videos of The School Of Life explain didactically about this, so I won't focus on this interesting behavior here. Suffice it to say that again it is about habitual behaviors, not interview content, even if they are so-called "bad" behaviors, such as habitual aggressiveness, rejection, coldness, detachment that a person may have and provide.

Returning to habitual behavior instead of interview content, it is curious to note that we want, then, what is habitual, and not the content that would fit into an interview of a few hours.

Einstein is the cliché example of brilliant interview content. His wife or spontaneous companion in general would admire not his content, but, I guess following this theory, would admire his good humor, or his dance to try to deepen, each day, that knowledge that even deepening always fits in a few hours of interview.

It is the dance, the everyday, that creates attractiveness in long relationships. I observe. I propose.

Here a new topic begins to emerge: novelty.

We are placing routine, daily habits, as the source of long-term coexistence.

How can we add novelty to the routine?

As we are analyzing, knowledge does not change, it always continues to fit into a few hours of interview, throughout life.

And does the routine change?

Here a question appears: even habitualness, the dance, the same gestures, the usual kindness, can also soon show their repetition, their little variability. Just as there is also, I propose, a lack of variation in our knowledge that fits in an interview.

So it ends up being left of my initial hypothesis that, if we need the search for novelty at certain times, this novelty should not come from the knowledge of a person that fits in an interview, because this is always a few hours, I propose. It is soon exhausted in coexistence.

But how does the dance, the gestures, feed a longer relationship?

Probably with the stimulation of senses and feelings.

Again, the knowledge that fits in an interview that each of us has is not capable of stimulating feelings in long cohabitations, because it is soon exhausted.

It remains the dance, the way of acting, but not the content. The way of acting, at the right time, creates a symphony of feelings in coexistence.

In this arena, the dance, the way of being, manages to replace our finite, which fits in an interview, knowledge, for long cohabitations.

We return, then, to our observation that I consider intriguing that someone's knowledge does not matter, at all, for long cohabitations. What matters is the way. The manner. Including the way of expressing knowledge, but not the knowledge itself.

For short relationships, then yes, the pleasure of discovering, during the first meetings, what the person has of knowledge that would fit in an interview, goes back to the pleasure of watching a beautiful interview.

I would even say that the pleasure is the same, whether watching a beautiful interview, or sitting next to a person and observing, for the first time, their content being gradually externalized.

Once the knowledge is exhausted, here is my hypothesis, the dance, the way of being, enters.

Then it's another person. It's another story.

It's another media, we could kidnap the language of communication for relationships.

We leave the interview for the dance.
