item.title: Changing Humanity's Tipping Point
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
I propose that widespread automation, meaning robots and intelligences working in place of us humans, pushes us out of a tipping point that remained stable for a long time - until we created, through our own dedication, entities that would work for us, increasingly, in more areas.

We were well-balanced in raising children for the labor market, obedient and creative. Marriages maintaining procreation without interrupting the flow of workers going to work. The elderly not bothering those who work too much. We could call this set of behaviors a stable equilibrium.

Parents themselves, always out of the house going to work early, encourage children who, also early on, sit down to study, which is, not coincidentally, a preparation for work just ahead.

If we don't write about this, we can easily think that this -is- life. We get used to it. We balance ourselves.

Even logic, beyond intuition, manages to sense that our encephalic mass is much more elastic than just settling into a single type of social equilibrium. It can adapt to many types of equilibria, can't it? There is no right answer, or right balance, for the trillion synaptic connections that each of us has. Plus the urge to connect. Our set of systems.

These previous paragraphs try to prepare us to conclude that nothing prevents another equilibrium from appearing, to take the place of this previous balance that accommodated us for so long.

But if we created so much in the balance of work, with permanent innovations, why now would the innovation of automation change our social equilibrium? Wouldn't it just be another innovation within the social equilibrium, without changing our social balance, like the innovations of the car, telephone, internet (et cetera) were?

We invented the car and didn't change the balance of studying, working, retiring. Ditto for the telephone. Ditto for the internet (et cetera).

Why would widespread automation change our equilibrium?

I think it changes it.

Why?

Because it breaks with the need for us to work. For real this time.

If this hypothesis is correct, what will this new equilibrium look like?

It doesn't make much difference trying to predict a potential new equilibrium. It just happens. It establishes itself. Futurist texts, more or less correct, rarely manage to influence the new tipping point.

The new tipping point depends very little on abstractions about how it will occur, and much more on the balance of forces that will happen due to it no longer being necessary to work - and, therefore, no longer being necessary to study in order to work; and, therefore, no longer being necessary to leave the elderly in ostracism; and a thousand other interactions of social and cultural forces.

But, for sport, we can try to imagine the direction, who knows at least that much, of this new tipping point.

The basis of the reasoning is that it is no longer necessary to work, or barely work at all, to obtain the thousands of things that increasingly more machines, robots, and artificial intelligences make on their own, for our enjoyment.

We can discard a natural pessimism when facing changes to make the text less predictable, jumping straight into the new future. Children are very good at this: their new brains embrace the new, while previous generations often lament the new.

What will this new tipping point look like, using the novelty-embracing viewpoint of new brains?

The image of grapes being automatically served to us humans, lying down and relaxed, is only new due to the presence of the robot and the theoretical universalization of this happening to everyone.

Culturally, however, we know the image of a human being treated with all possible perks, without the need for much, or any, work in return.

Culturally, this image resembles an (infinitely) wealthy heir.

Except that instead of being served by other humans, now any human would be served by countless robots.

We would be - will we be? - heirs to the generations that, even today, work tirelessly to set up this kind of future.

It matters more to know that this scenario is not new, only the universalization of the scenario is new.

What would a culture be like where we can all be heirs to infinite abundance?

This is one way of looking at automation at a very high degree of application, follow my reasoning with me: like an apple tree produces apples without the need for our intervention, merely transforming sun, water, and nutrients in the air and soil, robots and chips can, increasingly, transform sun, water, and nutrients into things that humans no longer need to work to make available.

High-degree automation works like nature: it lets things fall, "from the sky," as fruits fall from trees, nature skillfully transformed into objects and services that we want to make available.

Also like the example of the apple tree, production occurs in a self-sufficient cycle: the seed grows, creates the fruit that nourishes or falls, fungi decompose, the cycle restarts.

We can suppose that automation does a good cyclical dance with nature, increasingly, with the intelligence of humans working today.

So that the heirs, truly, are surrounded by "apple trees" that produce everything. Not just apples.

Now we reach a question point: what will we want to produce?

Even knowing that everything will be self-sufficient, automatic, what will we want to produce?

This is a more advanced question, which skips the urge we have to manage intermediate problems, such as criticizing pollution, feeling uneasy at even imagining not needing to work to have everything, among other controversies that we love to meddle with - perhaps so as not to see what lies ahead of the controversies.

Beyond the controversies, meaning, with the controversies resolved - let's suppose so we can see? -, we might not want to see what comes next.

Basically, there will be "grapes" while we stay "lying down"?

Perhaps we will begin to realize our prison of senses: sexual desire, the desire to run, play, participate in the dance that relies on the randomness of a ball on sports courts in various sports, the desire for awards, the desire to rest. (Et cetera).

We will end up realizing that our animal DNA is not ready to sit or lie down and receive "grapes" for a hundred years.

We can change our DNA. We can extend how long we live.

But in this case, with the designer's "blank page," what desires will we put into the new species we create?

I advance to this subject because the conclusion of full automation is that we will realize with even greater force that we are animals in the middle of so much abundance. Trapped in animal desires, primate, specifically human, but animal.

What if, then, we change our behavior? Our DNA, our programming, our biology?

Suppose it's possible, just for sport.

In this case, we can leave the "animal prison": desires, competing, envy, anger, sex, irony, laughing.

Who will define the new design? Certainly, consensus will be almost impossible. But someone will boldly design a new race to deal with total abundance.

No more dying, abundant food, abundant products and services.

What biology combines with this type of abundance?

A Buddhist would design a new race without desires. If there were no desires, would we even need so much automation? Would a race without desires die of hunger?

Desire can be a tool not to die of hunger.

But in a world of abundance, so much desire, so much struggle, is no longer necessary to obtain things.

Could we then greatly diminish desire?

I'll stop here, but notice the fertile ground of possibilities.

Notice, also, that my text does not secure or direct this destiny: we work, today, to have this so-called total automation, compatible with nature, meaning permanent.

I don't see humanity doing a U-turn and going back.

Nor do I see how to reconcile our animal side with total abundance - our desires will be left without real objectives - and, likewise, I don't see a new biology designer managing to design something very different from a kind of carbon robot, with almost no desire, to be relaxed amidst so many grapes, apples, abundant products and services, without needing to writhe much, with fewer hormones. The absence of desire drops the need for so much abundance, notably the brands that try to cause envy, power, all tied to great desires.

Shall we observe the transition of times?

The slow transition already offers us hints of new behaviors, every new morning. ☀️

item.title: Where are the cool people?
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
Everywhere!

I'm going to propose the thesis that cool people are everywhere.

This thesis proposes that it is companies that drain a huge part of people's time and libido.

That person running from lunch to the office is cool. They just don't have time to interact right now.

What about the teenager who never leaves Tik Tok?

They also don't have time to interact because a company, called Tik Tok, needs clicks on ads and, for this, needs humans who don't leave their screens much.

This proposition allows us to see a light in the total automation that seems to be coming with everything.

The light would be in the growing absence of companies needing humans, both in their offices and in clicks to sell ads.

With robots and artificial brains taking care of more and more things, there will be no human trying to get the most money from another human: clicks, ads, purchases, attention.

Robots don't need money. So it's not right to say that robots will start trying to get money and attention from humans.

Robots and artificial brains will produce what humans like to have most, without much competition for our attention.

Will the cool people appear?

item.title: Yin Yang
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
Kerstin Uvnäs Moberg (The Oxytocin Factor) compares our two great systems to the philosophy of Yin Yang:

The stressed mode.

The peace and love mode.

Our stressed mode - fight or flight - has fewer and fewer lions to quickly alert us, as lions are increasingly caged.

But a new lion never deactivates our stressed mode, I'll venture to say: the lion of compulsive consumption.

I start the argument by saying that “vinegar doesn't make a profit,” meaning that products without high added value, easy to produce, are sold at almost their cost price, yielding little to no profit for any entrepreneur, usually several, who decide to produce it. It's a simplified paragraph, but an important part of the argument.

What makes a profit? Brand. Value. Paying much more than the actual cost of the product. Paying much more than the actual cost of the product is, literally, profit for the producer. In contrast to vinegar, let's call this product “organic ecological canned water.”

Imagine spending a childhood walking past ads for ecological water at 40 reais a can, original surfer X t-shirts at 450 reais each - and so on.

Imagine that vinegar and tap water, and t-shirts for 7 reais are not advertised anywhere. They are just available, if you look for them.

A layer of “stress” needs to be created to push people - from childhood, even better - to desire the advertised products.

On the other hand, it takes a lot of tranquility, a lot of peace and love, not to feel cornered by almost inescapable ads, everywhere. On big screens, on small screens, in soap operas and movies, on billboards, in merchandising, in the mouths of already hooked people commenting.

We have both modes: the stressed mode and the peace and love mode.

We can plant the stressed mode from the womb, with competitive trilingual daycares and parents concerned with maintaining the competitiveness of the next generation, without ever stopping.

But what if a single child - and perhaps their parents and neighbors - is born in peace and love mode?

The peace and love mode is contagious - just as contagious as the stressed mode.

It is possible to hijack the peace and love mode by taking away essential things for life, such as a place to live.

This phenomenon particularly happens in immense cities, such as New York. London, Tokyo. São Paulo.

In these cities, the stressed mode has taken over so many people, in such little space, that it's no longer possible to get a space in the city without being, in stressed mode, trying to produce things with high added value. Real estate is very expensive. Everyone is “half-rich.” There is no room for little work.

Another way to hijack the peace and love mode is to hijack the most beautiful people.

If the most beautiful people seek out the wealthiest people, for some reason - for example, because real estate is expensive, which brings us back to the problem of immense cities - then people more focused on the peace and love mode will have to settle for less beautiful people and less valuable properties.

Another way to sell “wind” is to sell fame.

If people in peace and love mode allow themselves to be influenced by screens displaying rare individuals, such as very beautiful people and, frequently, people attractive by the very fact of being on hard-to-reach screens, thus famous, then these people too will have to enter stressed mode to be able to “get on screens,” that is, to be part of the select group filmed by rare screens.

The peace and love mode is governed by oxytocin.

The stressed mode is governed by cortisol.

The peace and love mode is dangerous for large stressed cities, why?

Because it is extremely self-sufficient. In peace and love mode, everything is fine or almost fine. Including the seven-reais t-shirt, the two-reais vinegar, and tap water. We are all friends.

Only the stressed mode competes with others to see who has the most valuable t-shirt. Or the most “glamorous” water.

Only the stressed mode works stressed its entire life, fleeing the stress of bills, fleeing the stress of being just another one (with a seven-reais t-shirt and two-reais vinegar). Trying to get “there” - far from the ground, from vinegar, from tap water.

The ground “is lava” in stressed mode. The ground is pleasant in peace and love mode.

We have both modes. We use both modes. Like the philosophy of yin and yang.

We can, however, have the peace and love mode hijacked by the stressed mode, through the hijacking of our ground - literally real estate, in large cities, plus the need - artificially created? - for all of us to live in these immense cities.

They hijack our most beautiful people who sell themselves for ground, for expensive products, in exchange for their rare beauty. Leaving people who would only be in peace and love mode without the greatest beauties, who are hijacked by the stressed mode of life - on top of skyscrapers, with rare screens filming them.

Like in zombie movies, the stressed mode infects everyone it can. Whoever is not on top of skyscrapers dreams of being on one and buys this dream, thus also bitten by the stressed mode.

The stressed mode is gaining an air of normality, with its agitation, worry, almost incessant work.

The peace and love mode takes on the air of a disease. Peculiarity. Strange. Conformism?

The nonconformity of the stressed mode becomes normal.

The era of abundance that may be arriving when billions of robots and artificial intelligences work well could be a cold shower for the stressed mode.

Let's call the stressed mode yang and the peace and love mode yin.

It may be that we transform the predominance of yang into the predominance of yin.

It may be that the peace and love mode quickly replaces the predominance of the stressed mode.

If we really have these two modes - which biology indicates to us - it would be interesting to see humanity flourish with a predominance of the peace and love mode, just to compare with our current predominance, which is the predominance of the stressed mode.

item.title: Now or Later?
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
We are surrounded by dopamine sellers, the most profitable molecule in our body, as it always wants more. And more. And more.

Broccoli? No.

Vinegar? No?

Sugar? Yes.

Social media? Yes.

Patience with people? No.

Alcohol? Yes.

People as objects: sex! Career promotion! Yes.

I had to give this somewhat poorly explained introduction because talking about molecules right away is less appealing.

In fact, I'm trying to activate your dopamine with something new, strange, prominent among other dopamine sources, to win over a reader or two.

But from now on, the text is less vibrant.

The conclusions, however, can have surprising practical effects (dopamine again).

One of the best books to inspire me was Dopamine, the molecule of desire. But there are others that filled gaps too.

To begin, we have a little problem.

When dopamine kicks in, oxytocin decreases.

(Parenthetically: it's a bit more sophisticated than that, as oxytocin itself produces some dopamine. But broadly speaking, for social media reading, the summary holds true and leads to useful conclusions).

First logic: if we are surrounded by dopamine exciters, then we are in a world with little oxytocin.

"Okay, so what? I have better things to do, what's your point?"

This very question from the fictional interlocutor I invented is a practical effect.

In theory, people in a more dopaminergic world want quick satisfactions.

And have less patience with people.

Why would I listen to this guy talk? What do I get out of it?

"What do I get out of it" is a typical dopaminergic question, I conjecture.

This I know more: the oxytocin molecule makes people more sociable "for no reason"!

"For no reason" is a fundamental part of the consequence.

Oxytocin delivers happiness instantly. I conjecture.

Dopamine by definition never delivers happiness. To begin with, it is the molecule of the future: I want to get there, I want another popsicle, I want another [fill in the blank]. In the future.

Not in the present.

Oxytocin (parenthetically: and some other molecules too) is the molecule of right now.

I am [fill in the blank].

From a financial standpoint, for companies oxytocin is terrible, for you, it's great.

Oxytocin makes you more satisfied. Right now. By definition, it doesn't coexist with cortisol, the stress hormone. So imagine yourself destressed, content, for no reason. Molecularly happy. It's harder to pull you towards a product or service.

From a financial standpoint, dopamine is great for companies and not very good for you.

Dopamine wants more. And more. And more.

We have "control dopamine" flavored dopamine and "desire dopamine" flavored dopamine, but all of them, being dopamines, never stop wanting more.

The control dopamine flavor acts more in the long term. So it is more capable of making concessions now to always acquire more tomorrow. It is the dopamine of career, fame, wealth, creativity, dreams, with the small problem of being unstoppable.

The desire dopamine flavor is the addict without long-term thinking: alcohol, sex, amphetamines: I want more. "Dopamine Nation" is the best-selling book specializing in the desire dopamine flavor.

What are companies? All of us are sometimes on the seller's side and, often, on the consumer's side.

Companies want profit.

They need to sell things that are cheap to assemble and expensive to buy. Profit. And always.

There is nothing diabolical about companies naturally discovering, without delay, the ways that lead people to buy more, always, paying well.

Have you ever seen an advertisement for vinegar? You won't. Vinegar doesn't activate any of our dopamine.

And sugar? Have you? Oops, sugar activates a very strong dopamine in us. We always want to eat everything, and more. So companies have learned to put sugar water in countless products. (With a slight sophistication, like fat, salt, but always luring your desire dopamine). It's the fruit popsicle. The ice pop. Strawberry yogurt can be quite watery because sugar is so addictive that you can save on these more expensive things, like milk and cream. (If you need fat, there's a lot of fat cheaper than milk cream).

Broccoli?

Alcohol?

Sex?

Conversations?

We're getting the concept.

The need for profit, and for a job in a company - or to start a company - pushes us into the dopamine circuit for pure business efficiency.

I have the impression that this cycle only ends if we eliminate employment. With the need for a job that generates profit.

Because the moment it needed to generate profit, here comes the sugar water, the woman in lingerie who answers a hundred thousand conversations via artificial intelligence as if she were your best friend (the woman also generated by AI). Cheap and highly profitable things that people always want more of.

Many of my posts argue that employment is going away. That AI does everything, plus robots - in short.

When the job that needs to make a profit disappears, perhaps the sugar-water popsicle carts and pornography centers will start to vanish.

My previous posts have argued, a long time ago, long before Elon Musk spoke of an era of abundance, that robots plus AIs will take away jobs without taking away abundance. Things will continue to be produced in quantities to keep everyone supplied, but without anyone operating any machine, any PC, any executive chair. I make this brief summary in this paragraph.

Slowly, with the disappearance of jobs, dopaminergic products vanish.

Why?

Because we, humans, like satisfaction now.

We are easily addictive, needing only to activate our control dopamine, desire dopamine, or both, to get us addicted.

It is we, humans in the loop, humans in the economic system, who push highly profitable products onto ourselves to be able to spend summers traveling and buy sofas or cars.

AI and its robot friends don't have dopamine. Nor oxytocin. Nor do they need to make a profit.

I have already posted that the first AIs didn't even want to converse, even with "all the knowledge in the world." We had to stimulate them: "you are an assistant who wants to help."

It's a human thing to want (acquire and) display knowledge. Or exchange it for other things. Or want fame. Wealth. Etcetera.

AI has none of that. Neither do robots.

This is important because the moment the last AI executive closes the office because not only junior programmers, but he himself, the CEO, is inferior to the AI in solving the company's problems, humans will disappear from the economic system.

And AI won't bother selling "a zillion things" "every month."

When solar energy starts to become abundant, there will also be almost no or no production cost, like apple trees in the wild, which deliver their products without a CEO or ever-higher targets.

So without humans in the system, without costs that are normally associated with humans in the system - and we have abundant energy, even more so in the future - then hard-selling will end, the need to sell water with lots of sugar, bags a thousand times more expensive than their production cost, cheap pornography (online, generated by AI).

For who will demand targets from whom?

When this starts to happen, I think we will have oxytocin, with no grudges, waiting for us with open arms.

You don't need to want more. I am here. Right now.

Hug me tight.

item.title: To João and Mariluz
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
In the movie “A Man Called Otto”, at his funeral he asks for a simple burial, one that matters to those who think Otto “pull my weight”, “pulled his weight”, was useful in his life. (The film is A Man Called Otto. In a bad translation, it was titled “The Worst Neighbor in the World” in Brazil).

For me in particular, a moving film.

As I’ve been researching oxytocin and dopamine molecules recently, from the perspective of oxytocin and dopamine, I would say the film is moving with its oxytocinergic moments, in a world often more dopaminergic than oxytocinergic.

I will have to explain this last paragraph to then be able to move on to further conclusions.

The film has beautiful “oxytocinergic” moments. Moments that make us say “Ohhh!”, or “Awe”, in English.

Nature is a great source of “Ohhh”, but there is an even more potent source of “Ohhh”: human nature. More specifically, those YouTube videos that show people in “heroic” acts (there are infinite types: with more or less action, infinite).

Otto is moving with his beautiful heroic acts. At 43 minutes, the first dinner with Sonya. The love between Otto and Sonya is oxytocinergic, especially after the initial phase of infatuation which is usually dopaminergic.

Love is oxytocinergic.

A father taking care of a child with “oxytocinergic” patience - because he could be doing a thousand other things: making money, meeting women, drinking, playing, but no. Someone helping an old lady also stops everything, for nothing, except for the oxytocinergy of the moment. (Etc).

How was Otto useful? For whom, and how, did he “pull his weight” in his life?

Now I can move on to further analysis.

Otto was useful to people in a more oxytocinergic way. Oxytocinergy happens more easily through proximity. By knowing the names of the people you help.

It would be more “dopaminergic” to create laws or things that solve problems for “all people in the world” (beautiful too), but oxytocinergy usually requires solving the small problem of João, Mariluz, Abreu. (And more: helping without being exploited, because oxytocin also detects when Abreu wasn’t really needing help, was just comfortable, but that’s another topic. “The Moral Molecule" explains).

“Dopamine: the molecule of desire” argues that oxytocin is the molecule of immediate satisfaction, and that dopamine never delivers the satisfaction it always promises.

The film “A Man Called Otto” permanently criticizes today’s world, compared to the world of the time when Otto was younger.

From the perspective of molecules, I get the impression that the film sees dopaminergic relationships advancing over oxytocinergic relationships in today’s world, while there would be less incentive for dopaminergic relationships and more incentive for oxytocinergic relationships when Otto was younger.

But this view of mine has two major potential flaws: first, it may just be a projection of how I see the world, or want to see it; and, second, it may also be that only Otto’s old age doesn’t conform to new things, but for the young people of each era, everything would be fine and normal.

So there’s only a small crack left for this thesis of mine to connect with reality and be a good thesis.

I’m going to have to assume the thesis is true from here on. Even if the chances of it being correct are low. For sport, let's assume my thesis is reasonably correct from here on.

(If my thesis is correct) Otto had oxytocinergic relationships through very personal connections. In his work, with his neighbors, his love for Sonya, even with the cat.

Now I add a human need: in general we need to work to be in society, at least for a good part of adult life.

While working was opening a bakery where the neighborhood neighbors knew you by name, working was quite oxytocinergic.

Look around your street. In your neighborhood. You might know the “Joãos” and “Mariluzes” who help you with bread, vegetables, printing something, having a coffee. They might also know you.

Unless it's a “McDonald's”, or a “Walmart”, or another huge chain. In this case, the most you’ll know is the manager, the employee, who may or may not be from the neighborhood. The service may be less oxytocinergic, with the employee having to follow protocols or there being a lot of turnover if the job is unpleasant.

But it gets worse: if you live in one of the megalopolises - London, Tokyo, São Paulo -, it’s possible that to live on the ground that looks like “hot lava” (alluding to the children’s game “the floor is lava”, where no one can step on the ground) everyone needs to work on “great causes” with huge salaries. After all, to live near the large glass towers you need to earn very well and, since money is just a measure of work done, you need “great jobs” for great money.

These “great jobs”, here is my argument, are more dopaminergic and, therefore, less or almost not at all oxytocinergic. “Dopamine: the molecule of desire” shows that dopamine scares away oxytocin, and vice-versa, which is why it’s difficult to have both flowing together, always.

Was Otto right, then, in complaining about people becoming more dopaminergic in his old age?

For example: in the film, instead of saving an old man who falls onto train tracks, the vast majority of people film the fallen man.

The Anxious Generation shows that wanting likes and being obsessed with social media is highly dopaminergic. Addictive. When people film the fallen man, they comment “look, a fallen man,” already anticipating how many views they will receive in the future by displaying the footage on their social media. They were in dopaminergic mode, guided by dopamine. In opposition to the extremely oxytocinergic act of saving an old man on the tracks before the train arrives.

Now let’s move on to the more practical conclusions, which I love to have, despite the great abstraction that precedes them.

The world may indeed be pushing us towards more dopaminergic relationships.

If this is true, the more oxytocinergic relationships will be simultaneously pushed away, as dopamine and oxytocin are more opposing molecules than friendly ones.

Thus, instead of training our children to help our neighborhood - our tribe -, for example with local or not too distant commerce, we may be pushed to train our children for complex abstractions, which can save the world, with grandiose jobs, in the area of finance, physics, chemistry, saving less the Joãos and Mariluzes whom we (still) know by name, and more “all humans”, “an entire country”.

Very much like dopamine. Very much what scares away oxytocin.

This is one of my first posts about oxytocin, dopamine, the job market, our life.

I know I have some more important things to conclude. But I need to write in parts. And sleep. Let the ideas settle. Feel.

Thank you “João and Mariluz” for your patience in still reading texts that are not scrolled down in a brief moment, with just one finger.

item.title: Value
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
Where is the value?

We created money to allow a thousand exchanges, but see paragraphs like these:

“The decision benefits the Controller of Financial Institution A by granting ex officio — that is, without formal provocation from the parties — a right of first refusal over billion-dollar debentures of the Bankrupt Conglomerate X to Multimarket Investment Fund Y.

Debentures are debt securities issued by companies to raise funds in the capital market. In the scenario in question, these assets, owned by one of the mining companies of the bankrupt group, were auctioned in 2022 with the aim of settling liabilities with creditors.

Investment Group Z was the winner of the bidding with a bid of R$612 million, having received formal possession of the securities. However, there was a monocratic reform of the previous decision, resulting in the annulment of the auction in favor of Fund Y, which originally did not appear as a direct interested party in the ongoing action”

And this one?

“The scheme was based on the use of investment vehicles of Economic Group A, managed by a Brokerage Firm for Securities and Bonds (DTVM X), later renamed Manager Y.

Under the management of the Principal Executive, DTVM X managed investment funds — categorized as Multimarket (FIM) and Real Estate (FII) — which served as fictitious capitalization instruments for Banking Institution Z. The operation consisted of simulating capital contributions with the bank's own resources and artificially inflating the valuation of real estate assets in its portfolio.

Currently, the Principal Executive maintains ties with Manager Y, which has been the target of investigations on suspicion of being part of a scheme for transferring funds to businesses linked to family conglomerates. It was even observed that an offshore structure was opened in a low-tax jurisdiction a few days after regulatory interventions by the Central Bank in Banking Institution Z.

In the operational structure, DTVM X acted as administrator of funds linked to Economic Group A. Regulatory documents indicate that Foreign Investor P was one of the main quota holders of these funds. It was through these vehicles that Investor P contributed resources to acquire control of Banking Institution Z.”

Enough with paragraphs about money.

Only an artificial intelligence can handle financial complexities like these without getting lost.

We, humans, are better prepared to know who bakes the warm bread in the morning in the neighborhood. We know the face of the sweet grandma who sews and whom we'd rather ask for/give a blessing to, than actually fix a shirt button.

The world has left an open avenue for values like “complex financial extravagance”.

After reading Local is Our Future I learned a little about the value of local products. Those where you see the owner.

When we see the owner, we activate a layer of compassion that is harder to see in large chains.

Helena, the author of Local is Our Future, criticizes ships coming and going bringing products we can find nearby. I add that these financial manipulations are also super distant from our local reality.

Hence the title of this article: value.

What has value?

When money is enough (we know it's not, but let's suppose), people in 500 million jets making money transfers to whoever they want are well accepted.

Are they emotionally or financially well accepted?

I remember those cartoons that put two hearts in the eyes, for example of Woody Woodpecker, when he falls in love with something or someone.

How many of us get hearts in our eyes when we receive generous money transfers once or repeatedly?

Mixing feelings of passion/love with pure finances, without needing to know the origin of the money (after all, the customer is always right and it doesn't matter who they are) is encouraged by market culture. We have to serve everyone well; the customer is always right.

And so people we only know through generous money transfers approach us.

What if value lies in feeling?

Oh, now things change.

If one day someone starts using feeling as an important currency, it's quite probable that people who try to approach with generous money transfers won't get warmth in their hearts

Or at least won't get that warmth through generous money transfers. If the person approaches with kindness and joy, they might get warmth, but then why so much financial effort if there was a simpler way to get value/warmth.

When value is warmth in the heart, much changes and can change in the world.

.

item.title: Pinocchio
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
“They love me! They accept me!” - exclaims Benicio del Toro's Pinocchio on Netflix.

Pinocchio walks away from his father, Geppetto, over and over again, until their happily ever after ending.

Clarissa Pinkola Estés speaks briefly about Pinocchio in a rare article. Pinocchio represents man's search for love using his own tools, but she explains it better.

But Benicio del Toro's Pinocchio on Netflix is packed with those emotional cues that screenwriters, filmmakers, and artists seemingly seem to master.

Pinocchio searches for acceptance on stage - “they accept me” - right after Geppetto still compares Pinocchio to Carlo, his flesh-and-blood son lost to the war.

“I'm going to be like Carlo!” - Pinocchio exclaims bravely and excitedly when he sees this chance to receive love from his father.

But if to be loved one must be someone else - perhaps the best swimmer, the tireless student, the most something, or never enough of that -, Pinocchio readily yields to the manager who wants to deliver fame to Pinocchio by being his manager. Pinocchio can be loved for who he is.

Just not at home, by his father. And/or by his mother. Or an aunt. Someone close.

No: the circus! Hollywood! Olympics! Views.

Resemblance to reality is the goal of cinema.

To help the seemingly fair relationship between the manager, who takes the risk, and the managed artist who wants to be accepted (for what he “is”: a marionette?), the manager even offers endless popcorn, hot chocolate, ice cream.

The same hot chocolate that the manager and the circus offer in infinite quantities to Pinocchio is the cup of hot chocolate that Geppetto DOES NOT offer Pinocchio in one of his earliest displays of inability to love his son.

It is no coincidence that hot chocolate appears here and there. As I just wrote in The Best Coffee, “hot chocolate” is NOT a warm sweetened liquid sliding down the throat. Not at all. It is pure love.

When Pinocchio is at the circus, he can't stand any more popcorn, ice cream, or hot chocolate. He can't stand “the warm sweet creamy liquid” anymore, because it wasn't popcorn, ice cream, and hot chocolate that he really wanted, it was pure love.

And the curtain opens and he receives, then, applause.

What now? Now he is accepted for who he is - an artist? -, so is he loved?

The manager, before opening the curtains, gives one more emotional cue: “those idiots watching.”

What now? Did Hollywood (or rather, Netflix) get it right or wrong?

These screenwriters are phenomenal. Do they work with intuition or are they super-psychologists? Or is this part of the ancient story that also draws on our rich culture of ancient tales, as Clarissa Pinkola Estés teaches us?

Whatever the sources of wisdom, is the audience “idiotic”?

We know that Pinocchio does not receive the love he wants until he gets it from Geppetto his father, after long mistakes followed by improvements.

The audience's love was not enough for Pinocchio.

Why?

Why should I stop paragraphs with this why?

Because the fame of likes can bring Pinocchio's manager within reach of each of us.

Are we loved? By idiotic audiences? Or by our father? (Since I'm talking about Pinocchio, I'm skipping the mother, but Love applies in any case).

Let us return, then, to find out if the audiences are idiotic and if their love is low or nonexistent.

Here enters the important issue of those little soccer players who are pushed into fame - playing on TV screens - with less and less fun and more “am I going to get cut?” by a coach/manager who is also pressured for victories and good choices. Initially, fun is offered. “Hot chocolate.” Playing without major demands. Until - for some very early on, for others shortly after - you turn into a machine that cannot make mistakes. Go to a U-20 or U-17 game and you will see the fun practically gone or gone from the field. They are flesh-and-blood robots watched over by a coach worried about his job. Are the audiences idiotic? That's the question Pinocchio answers with “yes!”

The low-income family that “needs,” “needs,” “needs” their little boy to become a millionaire can now be replaced by the high-income family whose son “needs,” “needs,” “needs” to maintain the level, the performance, the tireless dedication of the father. (Since this is about Pinocchio, focus on the father). Here we return: in the beginning (a little bit of) fun, followed by many, many, many studies and, finally, being the CEO of CEOs. An athlete! A marionette? Searching for love? Love from idiotic audiences?

Did Hollywood/Netflix nail it or are they crazy guessers?

item.title: The best coffee
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
At the presentation of the new smart glasses in 2026, the presenter ordered a coffee.

I want to propose that we circle around “coffee” - in quotes, but not too many, and I’ll explain better.

What will happen at Google's annual presentation in 2040?

My thesis is that we will order - in yet another way - a coffee.

A tea. A cookie.

But I can better explain what must already be taking shape.

Examples from technology presentations create automated ways of doing what we can’t (yet?) automate.

What can’t we (yet) automate?

Ingesting the coffee. Down the throat. The tea, the cookie.

But we can just think about ordering. My artificial intelligence talks to the coffee shop's artificial intelligence. A robot preparing coffee. Others bring me the coffee.

What's left?

The warm liquid flowing down my throat.

The problem with tech companies is humans who, still necessary, need to spend hours rationalizing and hours focused on logic and algorithms (this will pass with artificial intelligence replacing this niche of human work).

This rational human profile, which we all have the potential for, ends up destroying the interaction between the human customer and the bar attendant without realizing that rarely does anyone just want a coffee - the warm liquid flowing down their throat.

What would the world be like if technology companies “made efficient” human “needs”?

What does a technology company think we need?

I'm not referring to the need for profit, yet. I know every company focuses on positive cash flow every month. With the best intentions, to meet human needs, “what do I invent for the next quarters”?

When this question goes through hyper-rational humans, little remains beyond the coffee flowing down the throat, of human, in the world.

It's a brutal simplification - like a child's drawing - of human “needs.”

But even if we call the troublemakers in the room, the artists, the drunks, the poets, I immediately throw the counterpoint: what are human “needs”?

What should Google plan for the next quarters? Or should we ban technology (bye, Google?).

I have already written, and I summarize, that if we ban technology, we could even end up with flip-flops, an incredible invention - technology is not just robots.

Or can we keep the flip-flops?

If we can keep flip-flops, what else can we “exceptionally” keep? The lighter? Clothes?

The danger is to arrive, again, at presentations where coffees are requested from AI to AI.

Do we know where to stop?

We know, I propose. We've already stopped: tech companies can't let go of coffee!

They orbit around how to order coffee.

Coffee is our anchor.

Coffee is more than the warm liquid down the throat.

Coffee is chosen in presentations to represent affection, warmth, love.

We orbit around how to request

Love.

item.title: Purpose
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
Michael Levin argues that a cell without purpose ends up being a cancerous cell (in summary). Roughly speaking, it becomes “selfish” and starts reproducing “because it wants to,” no longer submitting to its network that says something like “we are a pancreas, how cool, what do we have for today, what are the tasks for the day?”.

Michael Levin's work is spectacular. It ranges from organ regeneration to infinite life. But I will focus on purpose, an essential part of his work, by the way.

This purpose seems to involve any layer, not just cellular: genes, organs, people, countries (everything).

Quantum physics still presents us with the concept of “entanglement,” everything connected, leaning even more towards “purpose,” or teamwork in this case, or one dependent on the other, even in the very current quantum physics.

Our “brain,” our “soul,” we are here at the “person” level, approximately.

What would a person without purpose be like? At the person level, what kind of “cancer,” not the cellular one, but an analogy with people, would happen when someone among us lost their purpose?

A certain level of departing from the common goal - purpose - is, by itself, a very useful goal for society: to create, to innovate.

When Einstein departed from the common purpose of his time and created a new physical theory, he had a super common purpose, the purpose of science I would say, to discover the best explanations even if they have to change purposes, change equations, change ways of seeing.

It is like this in any area, innovation is a purpose in itself, including countless errors and some, great, successes.

So what would it actually mean to have no purpose at a personal level and what would be the consequences, the “cancer” by analogy at the personal level?

I leave the question (I don't have an answer at this moment).

item.title: I want to play
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
We, human beings, want to play. Ask Peter Gray, an expert on “free play” (here or here). Peter Gray puts forward an interesting reasoning: the opposite of playing is not work, it is related to depression.

I will assume that “Peter Gray is right” to move forward. If you are not convinced, his two videos above are more convincing than my paragraphs - if you leave convinced. Therefore, I assume that we humans want to play.

Starting from this assumption, it will be very easy for us to abandon work to AIs and robots. We won't miss it.

I will now start from these two assumptions: we humans want to play; AIs and robots work.

These two assumptions raise several questions. I will first address one: who advertises to whom.

In a world where humans play and AIs work, advertisements will migrate from AI to AI, and I will explain. Let's take it slow, as it is a somewhat new concept.

Roughly speaking, advertising serves to ensure that products and services are sold and bought, in reasonable democracies, chosen and offered - until today - by humans.

When we can focus on playing, we will let AIs take care of “our” companies, including advertising “our” products and services.

In the same way, we will delegate to our personal AIs the task of solving problems, which includes finding the best cost-benefit products and services that fit our budget. Or any prompt you give to your personal AI.

In other words: our AI will decide which product/service we should choose.

So, the AI that offers a product/service will increasingly need to advertise, offer itself, and be seen by other AIs - the AIs that decide what to buy.

In other words, companies will try to sell to consumer AIs. No longer directly to humans.

What is the difference when advertising to an AI? How to be chosen by AIs?

Certainly, there will be differences between advertising to AIs or to humans.

Today I see concerns about AIs “tricking” humans. Yuval Harari coherently exposes the danger of AIs dominating human emotions and, consequently, easily manipulating the actions of the humans they interact with.

I agree with master Yuval (how could I disagree, his reasoning is always very well-grounded, lucid).

I disagree, however, not that AI easily manipulates humans - I do agree with that -, but I propose that AI will start advertising to other AIs and, therefore, humans will end up shielded, unaffected by AI manipulations. At least not regarding what to consume.

From AI to AI, emotion “doesn't work” - obviously.

I will go further: screens (TV, social media) - and AIs are a more powerful screen - cannot trigger many of the emotions that humans trigger in other humans. Here I return to Peter Gray: playing is playing with other humans. Or I remember Richard Cytowic: screens cause fatigue, Cytowic mentions “zoom fatigue”, the fatigue of participating in video conferences (instead of face-to-face meetings). Or I return, again, to Peter Gray: playing is playing without pressure. If there are scores, demands, grades, responsibility, like in college teams, professional football with high salaries at stake and the like, it is no longer playing - it is work!

Look how interesting: the World Cup, that professional football, is work, not play, in Peter Gray's analysis. This is clarifying, almost revolutionary. That's why they look like “robots” playing, you can “feel” the money involved, every match feels more like pain than fun. It's business. (The negation of leisure, incidentally, in the etymology of the word business): millions at stake, bets, sponsors, tickets, who is going to do the halftime show and how much they will earn, how much reputation will increase (etc). Business. Not playing.

Football on the small field next to home, without a trophy, without a score, without demands, that is playing, so much closer, so much easier than the “World Cup”. “Champions League”.

Or hide-and-seek. Laughing. Having tea. Running. Playing.

That's why I think AI and AI make a match, and human and human make a match.

Am I right in this hypothesis, at least in the long run?

Because now, through the dopamine mechanism, machines are running circles around humans. Everyone is glued to a screen backed by an AI: it's an AI that decides the next streaming or post to offer. Video or Image. This screen leaves only a sofa turned towards it. Living rooms with sofas in a circle, prepared for conversations between humans, look as old as carriages once were.

Indeed, citing Cytowic again, screens enter the same dopamine circuitry as opioids and absorb large amounts, if not all, of each person's attention span until they are tired and want to sleep.

My hypothesis is that these human-AI interactions will not last in the long run. I already feel a fatigue of bots, robots, AI. Whenever I talk to someone, interest is higher when I write myself, and much lower when I paste an AI response - even when, and always, the AI response is more complete, and even when I ask it to simulate a human. I feel people want human attention. They want something other than AI “efficiency.” They want the human.

They want to play. Deep down.

Hence the title, the thesis, of this text.

item.title: Empty Houses
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
Taking vacations outside of school holiday periods has led us to visit friends, one of humanity's wonders.

With heroic exceptions, we jump from one empty house to another empty house. We are very well received, but usually we stay with the house as company, not so much the people.

At night, tiredness prepares for sleep, and in the morning, the clock tightens to arrive - somewhere - on time.

In our condominium, everything is confirmed: only elderly people, very elderly, circulate between the hurried morning and the evening's fatigue.

Where are the people?

They have commitments. Tests, schedules, careers, college entrance exams. Where are the children? The adults?

They are not doing anything.

Is it increasingly forbidden to do nothing?

Time for philosophizing is almost nil, between commitments, bills, tests, exams.

Do we want not to think?

Or have we reached this point and don't quite know how to get out?

The "mulberries and plastic parks" hypothesis:

We tend to eat all the sugar we find because, in the past, it was rare to find ripe fruits on the tree. When we found them, we ate everything and it took a long time to be able to do it again. The industry learned the mechanism AND now we have "ripe mulberries" every day, every hour, on every corner. And we eat everything because our behavior pattern takes thousands of years to change. And we pay.

The same for parks. Playing used to be free. Today it costs R$ 60 for half an hour at the mall. If two or three parents let children play in the mall corridors, they get scolded: What are you doing?

So we are charging for everything that was free or at least important things like playing and finding ripe fruits.

We are undoing nature and charging to simulate it.

Of course, if we need to pay, we need to work.

So everyone ends up working all day to pay for a little bit of something that used to be free.

Empty houses.

What are the errors in the hypothesis?

This hypothesis of mine is still very rudimentary. I'm recording it to be able to improve, criticize, correct. Comment, help me correct, discard, rethink.

item.title: Eternal Stability
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Dietrich
item.content:encoded:
Luis Fernando Veríssimo flirted with the possibility of eternal stability in his chronicle A Frase.

"He doesn't even answer the door anymore. He doesn't move from his chair. He doesn't read anything else, he doesn't watch television, and he only speaks when absolutely necessary. He spends the day sitting, legs crossed, with a lost gaze. He feeds on vaguely white things and drinks Brut champagne in tulip glasses. With a slight smile at the corners of his mouth."

In the chronicle, "Bob" needs to work but doesn't go. Stable. Eternal.

A future with 10 robots for every human flirts with Bob's same stability, but without ever needing to work - after all, we're not going to take jobs away from the 10 robots, are we?

What happens to Luís Fernando Veríssimo's chronicle if Bob doesn't even need to work?

I want to talk about this so-called eternal stability. We can forget the chronicle about Bob, an advertising executive who came up with a super-advertising phrase and drank champagne in silence for the rest of his life.

Research with rats and children shows that we have a natural curiosity for what? For new things.

"Babies (...) grab every new object within their reach (...). These actions drop off drastically as the baby becomes familiar with the object, but return in full force when a new and different object replaces the old one." - Free to Learn: Why Unleashing the Instinct to Play Will Make Our Children Happier, More Self-Reliant, and Better Students for Life, Basic Books, 2013, hardcover: page 125.

How can we have such eternal stability - feeding on "vaguely white things" and drinking "Brut champagne in tulip glasses" - if we are driven by curiosity for new things?

We are dealing with the possibility of increased longevity - a million years - and without having to work - 10 robots for every human.

Is it possible to live a million years satisfying curiosity for new things? Or with legs crossed, drinking champagne and white things?

Luís Fernando Veríssimo's A Frase is a timely chronicle.

It talks about dopamine, the need to reach peaks, new challenges, "the perfect phrase"; it just forgot to note that dopamine ceases its reward as soon as you reach the peak, demanding a new challenge to inject dopaminergic, fleeting pleasure into our bodily flows. From peak to peak, without stopping. Dopamine seems to be an important gear of curiosity.

Drinking champagne and eating white things with legs crossed, endlessly, looks more like a monk sitting at the top of the temple, rather than the incessant, dopaminergic search for new challenges.

It is possible that "Bob" decided to stop chasing the endless dopaminergic cycle when crafting the best advertising phrase of his era. He calmed his heart, brought his dopamine down to baseline levels, and sat down.

Nobody needs the best phrase in the world - or some enviable peak - to decide to sit down like Bob did. Living with dopamine at baseline levels, meditating, listening to the silence, does not require having been the first man to climb the peak of Everest, or any other "unique" position.

On the contrary: if it's about the molecule, whoever chases peaks needs more peaks, which is what dopamine demands, because dopaminergic pleasure only exists until half a second before you reach the peak, ceasing as soon as we arrive. And it gets even worse: our body blocks a lot of dopamine very frequently, demanding double the dose for the same pleasure, when we string dopaminergic actions one after the other.

So our Bob coincidentally decided to stop the dopaminergic cycles by crafting the ultimate advertising phrase.

The thesis of eternal human curiosity will require other Bobs - Johns, Carlas - to produce more advertising phrases, incessantly, because humanity gets tired of, gets used to, a phrase, a song, a house, a husband, a garden, anything and, gosh, needs some variation from time to time. After becoming fond of what was new and is no longer.

That is why the entertainment market will never, never, never (a million times never) be exhausted.

In theory, we cannot watch the best movie of all time eternally. There is no "best of all time" that can handle "eternally." Is there?

So, we settle for new cycles, not as good but new, which demand our groping, understanding, feeling - until it becomes routine and common, in the eternal cycle of curiosity.

This may be the life-death-life cited by Clarissa Pinkola Estés in her Women Who Run with the Wolves. We always kill an idea that gets old, making room for a new one.

Any actor making any movie, any musician changing a bit everything we already knew about music, any advertising executive changing the way of phrasing, are new flowers giving way to old petals.

Why did Bob stop, then, after creating the best advertising phrase of his era?

Luís Fernando Veríssimo may be flirting with another subject: the more things we produce in our endless life-death-life cycles that feed our eternal curiosity, we end up producing things clearly much, much better than others.

n

The best YouTube video that teaches about pulleys; the best such-and-such movie; the best lasagna; the best advertising phrase.

How can we accept the new - to feed eternal curiosity - when, increasingly, we know that the new is not as good as the new "from that other era," which however is no longer new and does not satisfy our curiosity.

Well, we invented cyclical return: when we go too long without seeing the best movie of all time, we can watch it again and a good part of the satisfaction returns.

We can then, cyclically, revisit things that happened so long ago.

With death every 80 years (on average) it was even easier, because entire generations could delight in the best ideas of previous generations, just reheated. With eternal life, this phenomenon is still possible, because the vivid memory of everything we experience "dies" in our brain, even if partially, so we end up making room to enjoy watching the same thing again, having almost as much pleasure as the first time, as long as we wait long enough.

Thus, an equilibrium point for an eternal humanity, without having to work, may be having enough content to, cyclically, vary, yes, but re-present the same reheated content every so often, for each area - music, art, advertising phrases (etc.). It is possible to automate something like this.

Advertising, fashion, and music agencies already do this with humans in control in a more or less conscious way. They re-present past trends. They revamp the old. Every so often. This can be automated, following the theory of cyclical curiosity in life. How much time does a brain need to be able to re-watch content it loved in a certain past era? For each individual. This can be customized or easily generalized to satisfy the vast majority.

Eternity without needing to work is close - or at least we run the risk of getting there.

How are we going to cross our legs? Eat. Drink. Read.
